A Pauli structure consists of specific collections of Pauli matrices organized into a specific type of statistical conical light cone within a 2D real vector space. This study establishes that such structures are equivalent to unital completely positive maps acting on Pauli operators between different dimensions, representing their connection to a broader class of maps known as "Pauli channels." This connection allows for a representation of these structures as a convex set where each point corresponds to a distinct channel. Furthermore, the work extends the definition of these structures to contexts between arbitrary dimensions. Finally, the text explores the relationship of these structures to quantum states by interpreting them as a form of quantum correlation function.

Time-variant matrix issues are prevalent in fields such as control theory, neural computation, and time-series forecasting. This study introduces a specialized category of time-varying matrix problems situated within the domain of time-series forecasting and proposes a time-varying zeroing control framework designed to address them. The proposed solution involves two time-varying zeroing neural architectures (ZNNAs) capable of generating real-time, dynamic solutions. The first architecture, referred to as the Time-Varying Zeroing Control Framework for Time-Varying Multiplicative Time-Series Forecasting (ZCFF-TFV), utilizes an exponential decay function to predict the evolution of time-varying matrices. The second, known as the Time-Varying Zeroing Control Framework for Time-Varying Additive Time-Series Forecasting (ZCFF-TAF), employs a linear function to forecast dynamic changes in these matrices. The paper outlines the design principles for both ZCFF-TFV and ZCFF-TAF, providing theoretical analysis and numerical simulations to validate their effectiveness.

This paper introduces a novel deep learning architecture featuring on-off center-surround fields (OOCSF) that precisely and robustly enhances image classification. By employing dual paired layers—an on-center layer and an off-center layer with surrounding nodes—the OOCSF model generates distinct representations for foreground objects and background contexts, respectively. This design enables the network to focus on salient features while simultaneously recognizing background patterns, resulting in highly accurate and stable classification. Specifically, the on-center layer detects key features, whereas the off-center layer perceives contextual surroundings. Crucally, these layers operate in tandem: the connection from the off-center layer to subsequent levels is gated by the output of the on-center layer. This mechanism ensures background information is processed only when significant object features are detected, allowing the model to isolate essential content and filter out irrelevant background noise. Experimental results demonstrate that this precise, noise-resistant feature extraction yields superior image recognition. On the benchmark CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets, the proposed model attained accuracy rates of 91.1% and 75.1% respectively, outperforming the current state-of-the-art methods.

X-ray optical components are increasingly utilized in instruments designed for a wide field of view. This article examines technical strategies for refining X-ray optics for such applications, specifically addressing surface and figure accuracy, surface scatter, scattering effects, and alignment precision. It also explores the synergistic benefits of combining these approaches. Furthermore, the text outlines measurement methodologies used to validate these improvements and presents illustrative cases from recent high-performance, wide-field X-ray concentrators.

Twisted bilayer graphene (TBG) exhibits a reentrant flat band (RFB) when a magnetic field is applied, a phenomenon that contrasts with the band-broadening typically observed in disordered systems. This paper provides a theoretical explanation for the formation of this narrow band in TBG by adapting the magnetic Bloch theorem to the twisted lattice structure. We demonstrate that the magnetic flux threading each unitary cell of the twisted lattice becomes quantized at specific values, notably $n2\pi$. The emergence of this flat band results from the precise cancellation of Lorentz forces acting on the twisted lattice's unit cell. Furthermore, we illustrate that the width and position of these reentrant flat bands can be precisely tuned by adjusting the magnetic flux.

This paper introduces a novel neural network-based approach for embedding secret messages in binary images utilizing Long Short-Term Memory networks. Our findings demonstrate that the generated steganographic content maintains superior visual quality compared to existing methods. To evaluate this, we conducted tests on an extensive dataset of 100,000 images generated by DALL-E, using binary patterns as secret payloads. The results indicate that the proposed method surpasses traditional LSB replacement techniques in terms of image quality, achieving an average FID score of 10.35.

Unit commitment (UC) is a critical component of power system operations, involving the strategic planning of generator on/off statuses and output levels over a specific timeframe. Modern, grid-scale renewable energy sources, such as wind and solar, are increasingly integrated into UC frameworks. However, their unpredictable nature introduces significant modeling complexities, often necessitating the expansion of traditional UC models to accommodate these new variables. Consequently, solving these enhanced, larger-scale models becomes increasingly computationally demanding. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a learning expense model (LEM) designed to estimate computational solution times. By utilizing LEM to filter out easily solvable UC instances, power system operators can prioritize solving scenarios that require more extensive analysis, thereby optimizing resource allocation and improving operational efficiency.

The material $\alpha$-Li$_{2}$IrO$_{3}$ is a promising candidate for hosting a "pure" Kitaev spin-liquid state. This study investigates how uniaxial stress influences its magnetic properties and structural characteristics. We conducted magnetic susceptibility and specific heat measurements alongside X-ray diffraction and magnetization hysteresis tests. Structural analysis indicates that stress induces a phase transition from the low-temperature monoclinic phase to a monoclinic phase with different symmetry at approximately $T_{\text{C}} \approx 25$ K, a process driven by a dimerization-to-trimerization shift. This magnetic dimerization is linked to the collapse of the interplay between edge-sharing and corner-sharing iridates. Furthermore, stress suppresses the low-temperature peak in the specific heat, which is attributed to the formation of these dimers. Additionally, magnetic susceptibility data reveal a phase transition to a long-range antiferromagnetic (AFM) state at $T_{\text{N}} \approx 1.1$ K, which vanishes under stress. The AFM order is linked to the interplay between the Kitaev interaction and the bond-dependent Heisenberg terms; consequently, stress is expected to weaken this ordering.

The synthetic control method is a widely adopted technique for constructing counterfactuals in panel data, frequently applied to evaluate policy impacts. It generates a synthetic unit by synthesizing observed data from control units that resemble the treated unit. This approach has proven effective in numerous policy impact studies, though it has faced criticism for lacking a formal theoretical foundation. This paper introduces a theoretical framework for synthetic controls that relies on the concept of a latent treatment effect, which represents the true policy effect if it were measurable. By applying this framework, we derive a conditions set that ensures the validity of using synthetic controls for impact estimation. This framework also facilitates a rigorous theoretical analysis of the proposed recognition and inference procedures. Consequently, we demonstrate that a specific variant of the Abadie et al. (2021) confidence interval procedure is valid under these assumptions. Furthermore, we show that a proposed variant of the synthetic control recognition method by Athey and Sefton (2021) is supported by our theory. Finally, we illustrate the utility of this framework through a case study of the Oslo policy, revealing that our synthetic control method yields more accurate policy impact estimates than standard approaches.

This study addresses Gromov-Wasserstein (GW) divergence estimation for graphs with unknown structures. We introduce a framework combining distributed structure learning with secure estimation, designed to ensure that intermediate results remain confidential across all participants. Specifically, our approach integrates a distributed version of the Graphical Holographic Embedding (GHE) algorithm with the Private Empirical Risk Minimization (PMEM) methodology. Our main contributions include: (1) a distributed distributed structure learning algorithm capable of generating Gromov-form distributions of graphs with unknown architectures; (2) a secure GW-divergence estimation technique that utilizes local graph representations and the private minimization approach to guarantee the confidentiality of the computed distribution; and (3) experimental validation demonstrating that our method offers comparable accuracy to centralized counterparts while ensuring the security of local data structures.

This study investigates the influence of polarization on laser-plasma electron injection and acceleration mechanisms. Specifically, we examine how a self-steepling laser beam interacting with an underdense plasma affects electron dynamics. Under both linearly and circularly polarized laser fields, we observe that electron injection and subsequent acceleration are governed by polarization effects, leading to self-generated electromagnetic fields that actively control the motion of injected and accelerated electrons.

We establish new, state-of-the-art constraints on double beta decay and dark matter-induced transitions in $^{194}$Pt. This study incorporates both traditional and novel methodologies, including the most sensitive global limits on the neutrinoless double beta decay of $^{194}$Pt to date, alongside the pioneering application of directional detection techniques to this isotope. Our results yield a lower bound on the effective Majorana neutrino mass of $\{1.1, 1.2\}$ eV (encompassing isotropic and directional approaches) and set the most stringent boundary on the axino-nucleon cross-section for sub-GeV dark matter particles, reaching $\{1.1, 1.2\}$ eV (covering isotropic and directional scenarios).

We introduce an innovative approach for adding color to black-and-white images from unknown camera sources. Our method, called Cross-Camera Propound Colorization (CCPC), utilizes a query image and a complete training set comprising colored images from the same camera, yet excluding the specific sensor of the query. The core concept involves leveraging the structural correlation between image content and color information. We establish a unified representation for both black-and-white and colored images by employing a shared deep network architecture that processes inputs from identical camera sensors. To ensure robustness across different lighting conditions, we incorporate stochastic color jittering during the joint learning phase. The resulting model effectively captures the mapping between visual content and color. When applied to a query image from the target camera, we first generate an optimized representation and then retrieve the most appropriate color palette based on this mapping. Empirical results indicate that our method surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques in terms of performance.

This work investigates the generalized $n$-dimensional Hamilton–Ermakov equation, demonstrating that its autonomous form possesses an $n$-parameter Lie point symmetry group. The analysis derives the associated Lie generators, which are then utilized to establish a set of $n$ first integrals. These integrals consist of one conserved quantity, the $n$-parameter Lie symmetry generator itself, and $\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ additional constants of motion. Furthermore, the text identifies a Lie divergence associated with the Lie symmetry, which functions as a conserved integral. The validity of these theorems is confirmed by applying them to specific Lie subgroups, including the Lie translation group, the polar rotation group, and the polar reflection group.

The General Assembly of the United Nations maintains a continuous record of debates and discussions, known as Transport Feeds. These documents, characterized by dense academic language, are largely inaccessible to individuals with limited English proficiency and are difficult for persons with visual impairments or existing visual disabilities. Our research focuses on enhancing the accessibility of Transport Feeds through two primary initiatives: (1) converting the existing static Transport Feeds into an accessible format, and (2) developing a text summarization system specifically designed to simplify complex academic discourse. To achieve this, we created a new dataset named UTAiS, comprising 1,022 articles from the United Nations. Our analysis reveals a strong correlation within these texts, leading us to propose an accessible Transport Feed generation system based on recurrent neural networks. This system utilizes transformer-based encoder-decoder architectures to generate simplified versions of the original texts.

Standard prototypes typically rely on the assumption that data within a class is uniformly distributed, resulting in the computation of their mean. However, this simplistic approach often proves ineffective for numerous classification challenges. This study introduces a novel prototype learning mechanism designed to enhance the generalization capabilities of prototypes, particularly in the context of few-shot learning. The core of our approach involves optimizing a prototype learning function that minimizes intra-class variance while simultaneously constraining inter-class distances. The method is validated on several few-sample classification benchmarks, demonstrating consistent performance gains.

The paper demonstrates a novel version of the Goldstone theorem concerning a scalar field with potential $V(\phi)$. In this formulation, the symmetry involved is assumed to be continuous but strictly non-reversible, meaning it exists only within the space of the field's configuration and lacks a corresponding group structure. A key innovation is that our proof relies on specific properties inherent to such non-reversible symmetries, bypassing the application of the standard Euler-Lagrange equations.

A graph is semi-transitive if it satisfies four specific conditions: it contains no cycles of length three or two, and for every pair of vertices $u$ and $v$, if $v$ is not adjacent to $u$, then $v$ is not adjacent to all neighbors of $u$. These graphs are notable because they represent an intersection of three well-defined graph classes: irreflexive, asymmetric, and transitive. This property makes semi-transitive graphs valuable for modeling various phenomena, such as weakly connected preferences, dominance among similar entities, and causal links in time-series data. While these graphs are not inherently transitively symmetric, we demonstrate that every semi-transitive directed graph can be represented as the underlying undirected graph of two distinct semi-transitive digraphs. Specifically, the first class comprises digraphs where the asymmetry condition is relaxed to weak asymmetry, while the second class involves relaxing the symmetry requirement to weak symmetry.

This study introduces a new method for identifying the decay modes of hadronic tau leptons, employing a seven-layer deep neural network (DNN) that leverages optimized input features. By addressing the inherent complexity of these decays, this approach offers a more refined layer of detail than previous techniques. We executed our analysis using data from proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, gathered by the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider with an integrated luminosity reaching up to 139 fb$^{-1}$. Our findings demonstrate that the hadronic tau leptons transform most frequently into one-prong final states, followed by those with three. Furthermore, our approach successfully distinguishes between signal and background events with greater precision than existing methodologies.

As data volumes swell, the need for reliable uncertainty quantification in machine learning has become essential. While Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) are widely recognized for this purpose, their performance in standard classification scenarios warrants closer examination. This study evaluates BNNs across two distinct classification tasks: image classification and text categorization. In image classification, we utilize the well-established MNIST dataset, applying both exact and approximate inference techniques. For text analysis, we employ the 20 Newsgroups dataset to compare BNNs against standard feedforward neural networks (FFNNs). Our findings indicate that although BNNs outperform FFNNs regarding predictive accuracy, their uncertainty estimation capabilities are notably superior, a trait that makes them particularly valuable for large-scale data collection efforts like the News2 dataset.

We report the observation of intermodal Brillouin scattering in a solid-core photonic crystal fiber featuring a small mode area. This phenomenon involves energy transfer between orthogonal linear polarizations, driven by distinct effective Brillouin gain coefficients ($g_b$) associated with each mode. We observe that the coupling coefficient between these modes is significantly lower than the difference in their respective $g_b$ values. By treating the system as a differential equation, we model the resulting modal power dynamics and demonstrate that the observed experimental data aligns well with this theoretical framework.

We establish far-reaching generalizations of the so-called "foundation theorem" associated with B-type finite-dimensional complex sl(2)-based Coxeter groups. Specifically, we demonstrate that the commutativity of the associated Hecke algebra and the centralizer of a maximal torus within the corresponding simply connected, semisimple algebraic group is a necessary condition for the finiteness of the group. This result extends beyond the classical B-type to all Type B, D-type, and E-type finite-dimensional complex sl(2)-based algebraic group structures.

The Set-Union Knapsack Problem (S-Union-ORP) and the Budgeted Maximum Coverage Problem (B-MCP) are two optimization challenges that have gained significant attention in the literature. Both problems are characterized by their NP-hardness and strong resistance to polynomial-time approximation algorithms. This research introduces a hybrid local search strategy designed to tackle these issues, integrating a greedy initialization phase, a solution repair mechanism, and a neighborhood search component. Furthermore, the authors have developed a mathematical formulation for B-MCP and derived a 0.5-approximation algorithm for the problem, establishing it as the established upper bound for achievable performance. Empirical results from extensive testing on a benchmark dataset indicate that the proposed method outperforms existing heuristics, achieving an average approximation ratio of 1.03 for the B-MCP.

User attrition represents a significant hurdle for companies, particularly those in gaming, where retaining players is essential for long-term revenue. While existing literature often analyzes historical data to identify past churn causes, predicting future user attrition is critical for enabling proactive retention strategies. This paper introduces a novel approach to forecasting churn within internet gaming by leveraging machine learning and analyzing in-game behavioral metrics. Specifically, we utilize data from a large-scale multiplayer online battle arena (MOBA) to train a Random Forest model, which demonstrates high accuracy in predicting churn. Furthermore, we apply SHAP (SHAPley Additive exPlanations) to identify the specific game events that drive user attrition. Our findings reveal that losing consecutive matches is a primary factor in churn, while the likelihood of winning increases with a larger pool of active players in the network.

This work examines the field theory describing Ising model dynamics within two dimensions under an intense transverse trans-Y Lee magnetic field. The study details the renormalization of non-linear sigma models, specifically focusing on how the fixed point of the Yang-Lee criticality arises.

We present an analysis of the electromagnetic interaction between low-momentum virtual electron-positron pairs and heavy ion nuclei in ultra-peripheral ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions. This study demonstrates that low-energy photons interacting with low-momentum pairs are strongly influenced by the finite nuclear size effect. This sensitivity provides a novel channel for pair production that could be detected in future experiments.

Cyclists are increasingly recognized as vulnerable road users, and their high risk of accidents involving near-misses demands advanced assistance. To address this, we introduce a novel video-driven risk identification system for cyclists that leverages near-miss data to enhance detection accuracy. This system incorporates a cycle-driven and video-based deep learning model capable of automatically identifying cyclists within video streams. Furthermore, we developed a cycle-driven deep learning model that significantly improves detection precision by focusing specifically on the cyclist's bike structure. Experimental results demonstrate that our cycle-driven approach achieves an mAP of 0.862, surpassing the best existing baseline by 0.032. To accurately assess risk, we designed a video-driven deep learning model that locates potential collision zones and quantifies risk levels based on the spatial distance between the cyclist and obstacles. This video-based method attained an mAP of 0.813, exceeding the top baseline performance by 0.023. Finally, we refined the risk identification model by integrating contextual data regarding cyclists' speed and direction, which yielded a further improvement in both precision and recall.

This study introduces a motion planning framework for robotic systems operating in unstructured environments that explicitly accounts for both control barrier functions (CBFs) and safety-optimized path generation. By integrating CBFs with model predictive control (MPC), the MPC formulation incorporates constraints that guarantee collision-free navigation while ensuring adherence to specific control policies. Furthermore, the method employs probabilistic constraints to enhance the approach's robustness against disturbances and uncertainties. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of this system in navigating uncharted spaces and identifying safety-optimized trajectories.

Let $R$ denote a ring whose unity need not exist. The **encompassing number** of $R$, symbolized as $\epsilon(R)$, represents the maximum count of subrings (also needing existence for their unities) that can be chained such that each is properly contained within the next. This article establishes that every natural number $n$ can be realized as the encompassing number for some ring. Furthermore, we examine the encompassing numbers of groups and monoids.

Resilience in deep learning refers to a model's ability to maintain high performance despite encountering adversarial examples. While existing research predominantly relies on specialized, data-driven methods to achieve this resilience, we introduce a data-free approach that aligns with the model's architecture. This new method offers data-independent solutions to maintain robustness against malicious inputs. Our approach is grounded in the observation that the number of adversarial examples within a specific region of a model's feature space remains constant regardless of how that region is partitioned. Leveraging this insight, we developed a novel optimization strategy that maximizes resilience without requiring an explicit classification task. Empirical results demonstrate that a model trained with this data-free method exhibits superior resistance to both unseen and known adversarial samples, effectively outperforming current data-driven techniques.

We examine congestion differential equations featuring a general function $f$ and its associated singularly perturbed nonlocal counterpart, where interactions are defined by a kernel $f$. Our work establishes the existence of unique, globally Lipschitz-continuous, entropy-satisfying solutions for both the local and nonlocal equations. Our characterization of admissibility for these nonlocal systems is defined entirely through properties of the generating function $f$ and is consistent with prior energy-based findings by Li and Zhang. Additionally, the results confirm that local solutions emerge as the limit of both nonlocal variants, with the rate of this asymptotic convergence being dictated entirely by the chosen nonlocal kernel structure.

Gaussian fields are widely utilized as spatial random models across various disciplines. Although marginal distributions are often straightforward, they are rarely sufficient for practical applications. In many cases, valid inference requires conditioning on specific observations, such as those from noisy sensors. This study introduces a general methodology for conditioning Gaussian fields along arbitrary paths, with a particular emphasis on scenarios where data is available only at non-regular locations like rational points. The approach involves constructing the field by conditioning on a dense subset of the domain and subsequently taking limits, with the method's validity established through several representative examples. The authors demonstrate that the resulting conditional field exists uniquely, provided the Gaussian structure is defined by a suitable covariance kernel and the conditionals are taken in the sense of distributions. The method is illustrated using applications to one-dimensional Brownian motion and Gaussian white noise, with the final section presenting numerical experiments that confirm the approach's effectiveness.

This paper examines a ground-level sensor network designed to detect wildfires, supplemented by an aerial drone equipped with its own sensing capabilities. The system operates by having ground sensors transmit fire-related data to a central hub, which then alerts authorities. Simultaneously, the drone captures fire imagery and sends this data to the same hub. A key aspect of the network is that the aerial drone acts as a relay node, forwarding all data captured from the ground up. This study investigates the trade-off between increasing the density of ground sensors versus deploying a more capable drone, specifically analyzing how these configurations impact overall network performance.

The Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) is a flagship initiative at Fermilab, designed to deliver a transformative new era for neutrino physics. By utilizing a massive liquid argon time-projection chamber situated 1,300 kilometers away at an underground site, the experiment captures a neutrino beam generated from the decay of protons that oscillate into muons. This immense baseline allows DUNE to probe the profound question of whether neutrinos are their own antiparticles, a discovery that could illuminate the source of cosmic matter. Additionally, the experiment will measure neutrino oscillations over shorter distances, offering a precise test of the CPT theorem and a detailed understanding of neutrino oscillation patterns. These capabilities will significantly enhance our comprehension of neutrino oscillation phenomena.

The presence of heavy, unstable particles, such as supersymmetric partners, within nature is frequently signaled by final states characterized by large transverse momentum jets. To identify these heavy particles, top quark tagging is essential, and its performance is often constrained by the presence of additional top quark decays in events. This study introduces a new top tagging algorithm that effectively mitigates this contamination. By training a neural network on subjet kinematics and applying the Efficient Non-Parameterized Top tagger (ENTP) to ensure robustness against variations in jet energy, this top tagger demonstrates strong results. Furthermore, utilizing Shapley values to interpret the model's decision logic, we confirm that the enhanced tagger achieves superior top identification through improved discrimination power.
This work outlines the integration of a refined ontology for Vocabulary Objects (VOs) and introduces a proposed standard for VO enhancement.

We introduce a novel approach called Variance Decrease based Experience Replay for Policy Enhancement (VDE-ERPE), designed to address the issue of inefficient data utilization in Experience Replays (ERPE) within Deep Reinforcement Learning. In these algorithms, data collection occurs in batches, and Experience Replays store past observations to allow agents to learn from them. While this setup enables the training of agents in environments that are too complex or dangerous for direct real-world interaction, a significant drawback remains: as the replay buffer fills, newly gathered data is frequently discarded, leading to wasteful sampling. We address this inefficiency by applying techniques from Batch Varying Data Enhancement (VDE) to the ERPE framework. Our proposed method reduces the variance in gradients associated with older stored data, thereby improving the stability and sample efficiency of the learning process. Empirical results demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, achieving a marked boost in sample efficiency.

The study offers a comparative examination of two distinct methods for generating fermionic path integrals, namely the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and superbosonization, within the context of massless Dirac fermions in 2D and 4D. It is demonstrated that these approaches are equivalent when applied to abelian gauge theories; however, in nonabelian gauge theories, discrepancies emerge, particularly concerning the integration measure. Furthermore, an analysis of two-dimensional colorful Dirac fermions interacting with nonabelian gauge fields reveals that the superisotopic version of the path integral yields a level of universality absent in the Hubbard-Stratonovich formulation.

Spatiotemporal predictive learning is a critical component of machine learning, addressing the challenge of forecasting future states from historical spatiotemporal data. However, this task is notoriously difficult due to the inherent complexity of real-world state evolution. While recent years have seen a surge in research for such learning, existing methods often fail to effectively capture the motion characteristics embedded within historical data, leading to suboptimal prediction accuracy. To address this gap, this paper introduces a new framework, MoDeRNN, designed to extract spatiotemporal motion insights to enhance prediction performance. MoDeRNN employs a motion decomposition module that isolates multiple distinct movement patterns from historical sequences, enabling the subsequent recurrent neural network to model the future state for each specific pattern. We illustrate that the process involves an "intermediary" state where a neutrino from a nucleon annihilates with its antipode from another nucleon, resulting in a net zero neutrino count and leaving only two nucleons behind. Difficulties in modeling diffused tsunami wave propagation from asteroid impacts stem from the inability to define a source term within the shallow water equations. This study introduces a method to explicitly calculate these waves, utilizing the conservation of fluxes to simulate wave travel over time. This approach models the source term as a one-dimensional expanding spherical shell, with initial flux values derived from the complete vaporization of an asteroid. We present JWST data for 11 luminous ($L_{\rm IR} \geq 10^{11} L_{\odot}$), optically faint ($M_{\rm AB} \geq 24.5$) infrared-luminous galaxies (ILGFs) located at $0.1 < z < 0.5$. These objects, which are often overlooked in traditional surveys, are analyzed using JWST NIRCam observations to determine their stellar masses, star formation histories, and dust properties. The analysis reveals that 9 of the 11 galaxies host obscured starbursts occurring within massive halos ($\log(M_{\rm stellar}) \geq 11$), a finding confirmed by SED modeling that indicates significant dust attenuation ($A_V \geq 5$ mag) and ongoing star formation. These findings underscore the critical role of IR-only surveys in capturing the full population of star-forming galaxies and refining our understanding of galaxy evolution.

This paper investigates decidability and computational complexity within reduction and weakening hypersequent substructural logics, specifically focusing on implications formed by these logic variants. Our approach relies on a sequent calculus derived from a specific algebraic semantics—a right action monoid featuring a designated element that functions as an absorbing zero. This framework encompasses both intuitionistic and weakening implication reductions as special cases. We demonstrate decidability for logics adhering to additional constraints on the absorbing element, such as idempotency or absorption, and establish upper complexity bounds of PSPACE for reduction and coNP for weakening reduction, both applying to their respective implication logics. Conversely, we prove that the weakening implication logic is undecidable whenever the weakening absorbing element exceeds 2. These findings extend and refine earlier complexity results regarding contraction-free and weakening implication logics found in the work of Pichtel, Carames, and Pichtel.

Classification tasks involving unstructured data, such as images, are often modeled using embedding spaces where class labels are represented as one-hot vectors. While the neural tangent kernel has established that optimal solutions for fully separable data place these labels on a sphere, this approach suffers from label collision, where samples from different classes may map to identical vectors. We introduce HyperExpan, a novel labeling framework that maps labels onto the surface of a hyperbolic space, specifically utilizing the Poincaré ball model. This method avoids label collision and maintains a compact label space. Furthermore, we prove that the optimal HyperExpan solution aligns labels equidistantly, maximizing the margin between classes. Empirical evaluations on various visual and text-based benchmarks demonstrate that HyperExpan surpasses conventional baselines in boosting both accuracy and robustness against adversarial attacks.

This study examines how non-covalent interactions in dimers are altered by external electric fields, focusing on the S66 set of 65 small systems. We employ supermolecular calculations alongside high-level composite methods to assess these effects. Our findings indicate that the magnitude of electric field-induced changes in binding energy is highly dependent on the specific dimer, ranging from 0.01 to 0.5 kcal/mol. Analysis reveals that non-covalent systems with weaker initial binding energies and shorter equilibrium distances are more sensitive to such perturbations. Additionally, we explore the physical origins of these perturbations, highlighting the role of electric field-induced dipole contributions alongside modifications to charge-transfer mechanisms.

This study introduces a scheduling approach for Industry 4.0 environments that leverages real-time data to refine a scheduling algorithm. A key innovation is the modeling of ambiguity regarding machine availability, which allows the proposed system to treat scheduling as a set of decisions categorized into two types: definite actions made with full certainty and probabilistic actions made according to an ambiguity distribution. The objective of these operations is to minimize the expected total cost of processing and the impact of delays. The resulting algorithm is designed to be computationally efficient, enabling the processing of large-scale scheduling problems. Its performance is evaluated against a baseline that relies on deterministic assumptions, demonstrating that the proposed method yields lower costs in both definite and probabilistic operational scenarios.

This work proposes a new definition of robustness for cyber-physical systems (CPSs) based on the Signal Temporal Logic (STL) framework. Our robustness metric accounts for both temporal and spatial perturbations, offering a more comprehensive assessment of system behavior. Our first contribution is the definition of robustness for hard-time constraints, followed by the generalization of this metric to all STL formu-lations through logical connectives. We demonstrate that our data-driven robustness measure can be reformulated as either an optimization problem or a decision task, enabling the use of existing verification tools. Finally, we validate our approach using a simulated robotic arm scenario.

This study explores the nature of shadow matter, hypothesizing that it represents antimatter. To investigate this, a neutron-positron annihilation experiment was conducted using a high-intensity cold neutron beam and an antimatter probe equipped with accelerometers. The findings revealed that the produced antihydrogen atoms predominantly remained in a single, specific quantum state rather than existing as a thermal equilibrium. Furthermore, analysis of the accelerometer data demonstrated that this shadow substance interacts gravitationally in the opposite direction compared to ordinary hydrogen. Finally, the study presents a novel theoretical framework for understanding this shadow matter, highlighting its distinctively non-thermal nature and its propensity for gravitational repulsion.

We investigate the $\sigma$-tensor of the nonlinear diffusion equation $\sqrt{-1}\frac{\partial}{\partial t}u=\Delta_{\infty,u}u^{\frac{p-1}{q-1}}$ on a complete Riemannian manifold for dimensions exceeding one. This equation generalizes the case where $q=1$, corresponding to the Gross equation $\sqrt{-1}\frac{\partial}{\partial t}u=\Delta_u u$. Within this framework, we establish the existence of gradient approximations for both local and global solutions of the diffusion process.

We present a statistical analysis of 1,000 randomly selected, statistically significant, faint ($<1$ mJy) radio sources from the 1.4-GHz 1Jy Bright Source Catalog (1Jy Bright Source Catalog) to determine their characteristics as a function of angular size. This study employs image stacking to create an average spectrum and spatial distribution map for these sources. The resulting spectral data were fitted with a power law, yielding an average spectral index of $0.7 \pm 0.1$. Spatial distributions were modeled using exponential decay profiles with an angular scale size of $0.1 \pm 0.01$ degrees; notably, the spectral index increases with source angular dimensions. These findings suggest that the observed trends are likely due to the source population being dominated by radio galaxies rather than quasars.

Concealed Markov Models (CFMs) are defined as probabilistic generalizations of Boolean automata, where the counts of accepted input words are modeled using hidden Markov models. This study introduces a formal derivation of CFMs as a means to support QDF (Quantitative Data Flow), a programming paradigm designed to handle such counts. Specifically, we utilize the algebra of monads to construct a category of CFMs that exhibits the essential data-flow properties required for QDF. The work also provides a monadic framework for the structural analysis of CFMs, including the derivation of their closure under composition and other operations. The foundational concepts of QDF and CFMs are briefly reviewed in the accompanying paper.

This work examines the nonlocal characteristics of the most unstable and the highly dissipative components within the temporal evolution of one-dimensional turbulence driven by periodic boundary conditions and nonlinear viscous forces. By analyzing the co-occurrence of fluctuations across multiple scales, we demonstrate that these two structure types exhibit statistically significant correlations. Specifically, the data indicate a bidirectional relationship: both the presence of extreme small-scale activity enhances the likelihood of observing large-scale dissipative patterns, and conversely, large-scale dissipative structures increase the probability of small-scale turbulence. Furthermore, the magnitude of the dissipative structure's amplitude correlates with the intensity of small-scale turbulence, while the spatial extent of the dissipative structure is inversely proportional to the spectral wavenumber where small-scale turbulence peaks. These findings suggest that large-scale nonlinear viscosity facilitates the creation of dissipative structures, which subsequently act as sinks for turbulent energy, thereby amplifying fluctuations at fine scales.

We introduce a straightforward and adaptable framework for scattering phenomenology that connects experimental observables with fundamental theory. This approach centers on a "labelling" system for amplitudes, utilizing a tensor order parameter to classify them. This system naturally extends to composite operators formed by multiplying fundamental building blocks. By employing tensor algebra, the resulting formalism streamlines the connection between measured observables and theoretical amplitudes, significantly reducing the computational burden on both phenomenological analyses and theoretical calculations. We demonstrate the utility of this method through a case study of $B \to \pi \pi$ decays, showing its applicability to various physical scenarios.

This work examines the thermal equilibrium between a vacuum cavity and a black body, accounting for both Cavity mode restrictions caused by the effect and Cavity-Body interactions based on the principle that the radii of Cavity influence the spectral distribution of emitted radiation. We analyze how the size of Cavity impacts the total energy density, pressure, and temperature dependence of a photon gas inside, showing deviations from standard results when compared to the infinite limit case. We also explore implications for experimental observation and theoretical consistency with quantum field theory in confined geometries.

We introduce a privacy framework for conditional expectations, designed to mitigate information leakage regarding a reference distribution. This approach is adaptable to various privacy metrics, including $\epsilon$-divergence, $\epsilon$-fuzzing, and $\epsilon$-release. We examine conditional expectation calculations within the context of location tracking services, demonstrating that our methods effectively limit the exposure of user location data.

Autonomous systems rely heavily on 3D localization, a critical component for safe navigation. While current methods are often computationally expensive and slow, the Normal Distribution Transform (NDT) algorithm offers a compelling alternative by delivering rapid, globally consistent results with high precision. However, its reliance on closed-form solutions restricts its use to single static environments, preventing application in dynamic settings populated by moving obstacles. This work introduces NDT-Transformer, a novel framework designed to track moving objects in real-time and generate refined 3D poses. The system leverages multi-frame data to estimate object trajectories, enhancing localization accuracy. Experimental evaluations across both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate significant performance gains, with the method achieving an 80% reduction in registration errors and a 3.5-fold increase in speed relative to standard NDT implementations.

This study investigates how multisite fMRI data collection influences the statistical reliability of connectivity metrics and prediction accuracy for brain states. Using advanced machine learning techniques, we developed a pipeline to create predictive models of individual differences in resting brain activity. These models were constructed and validated on resting-state fMRI data from 1,041 participants across eight sites within the Human Connectome Project dataset. Our findings reveal that while large sample sizes are crucial, they alone are insufficient to guarantee high confidence in predictions. Furthermore, the quality of data collection significantly impacts both the strength of brain network connectivity and the precision of multivariate models.

In beeping networks, all nodes communicate via a uniform one-bit signal, or "bee," and remain silent during their turn. This paper presents a new bit-peeping protocol for node identification and power conservation. By integrating the existing randomized assignment bee with a deterministic broadcast beeeping algorithm, we achieve two key objectives: the self-assignment of unique IDs to every node and the transition of idle nodes into a low-power sleep state. Our approach ensures that during the broadcast phase, only active participants transmit signals while others efficiently enter sleep mode. We have formally proven that the algorithm converges in a polynomial number of beeps, successfully assigning IDs and activating the sleep mode. Furthermore, we have empirically validated our system through comprehensive simulations.

Code mixing is a prevalent and historically significant phenomenon within linguistics, yet the rise of code-switching and -mixing environments has introduced new hurdles for Natural Language Processing (NLP). This study introduces a code-mixing corpus comprising over 1.5 million sentences of Hindi-English mixtures, annotated with both language identification (LI) at the sentence level and phrase-level part-of-speech (PoS) tagging. Leveraging this dataset, we introduce PESTO, a Code-Mixing position embedding model designed to overcome the inadequacies of existing solutions. Our analysis reveals that current models fail to account for the dynamic nature of code mixing, particularly the shift between monolingual and bilingual states. To address this, PESTO incorporates two distinct positional encodings: Absolute Positional Encoding (APE) for sentence-level position and Relative Positional Encoding (RPE) for intra-sentence distance. Furthermore, to capture the dynamic nature of mixing, we propose Transition Point-based Dynamic Positional Encoding (TPDPE). This mechanism dynamically adjusts positional representations based on the location of transitions between the two languages. Experimental results demonstrate that PESTO achieves a 4.5% accuracy gain in sentence-level LI and a 4.1% improvement in phrase-level PoS tagging compared to the strongest baseline, establishing a new state-of-the-art standard.

Using the first-principles approach, we investigated how varying pressure influences the isotope effect and superconducting critical temperature ($T_c$) in superconducting H$_3$S. Our findings indicate that increasing pressure weakens the isotope effect, a behavior attributed to the shifting S-H bond length and its subsequent effect on electron-phonon coupling. This paper introduces a new technique for generating motion plans in dynamic environments populated with spatial restrictions. The primary challenge lies in the unpredictable interactions between the moving agent and these restrictions, which can alter the environment's topology and obstruct navigation. By accounting for every potential restriction state, the algorithm ensures a feasible trajectory is identified regardless of the configuration space's complexity. We have investigated the nematic instability in LiFeAs, a ferropnictide, by measuring the nematic susceptibility ($\chi_{nem}$) through the difference in resistivity along orthogonal axes. Our findings indicate that $\chi_{nem}$ increases with decreasing temperature, rising by a factor of 2.5 from 300 K to 20 K. This trend contradicts theoretical predictions for a nematic instability, which would require susceptibility to increase by a factor of 5 or 5.5 over the same temperature interval. These results suggest that LiFeAs does not exhibit a nematic instability.

The phenomenology of the Two-Higgs-Doublet Model (2HDM) is highly sensitive to its parameter space, particularly when experimental data is limited. This study examines how the global viability of the 2HDM framework will evolve with anticipated results from upcoming collider experiments. To address this, the authors have performed worldwide scans of phenomonena-related observables for both the Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (NMSSM) and the general 2HDM, utilizing the FeynHiggs and FlexibleSPheno packages, respectively. These analyses incorporate projections for the HL-LHC, FCC-ee, FCC-hh, and the proposed ILC. Furthermore, the investigation includes a detailed investigation of the CP-odd Higgs mass ($m_{a}$) and the Higgs production cross-sections at the HL-LHC, focusing specifically on the influence of the fine-structure constant, the top quark mass, and the top quark Yukawa coupling.

We introduce a neural network-based framework for modeling particle interactions, which allows for a procedure capable of assembling complex target structures from particles with minimal optimization. This methodology employs a specialized neural network potential to define the forces between components, ensuring that the resulting particle properties facilitate self-assembling behavior. The complexity of both the potential parameters and the simulation setup is significantly reduced through a neuroevolutionary training process. This evolution-based approach simultaneously trains the procedures for assembling structures and the particles themselves to ensure their effective mutual interaction. The methodology's versatility and effectiveness were demonstrated through the construction of various architectures, ranging from a single target structure assembled from particles of differing sizes to the simultaneous formation of multiple structures in simulation boxes containing heterogeneous particles.

We examine chiral gauge groups with the aim of establishing both robust anomalies and theory stability against anomalies. To achieve this, we employ the index theorem on index3 manifolds alongside a representation-by-representation analysis of the Green-Schwarz mechanism. The analysis reveals that a single $U(1)$ factor admits no anomaly-free configurations, whereas multi-component $U(1)$ theories admit multiple distinct free configurations that remain robust against high-energy physics. The analysis further demonstrates that multi-component $U(1)$ theories can be consistently embedded within larger non-abelian groups, such as $SU(5)$ or $SO(10)$, that possess standard robustness and anomaly-free properties.

This study examines the pressureless and full-system versions of the steady Navier-Stokes equations within critical Besov spaces. We establish global well-posedness for both the pressureless formulation and a specific initial condition of the full system. Conversely, regarding the complete well-posedness of the full system, although well solutions exist, they may grow unboundedly.

We introduce a microscopic model describing how light-excited magnons in dielectrics interact with phonons and thermal phonons. This interaction leads to the compression of the magnon distribution, which in turn generates temperature-dependent shifts in the nonlinear spectrum. To support this, we present a set of equations that describe the evolution and equilibrium state of a compressed magnon distribution. This theoretical framework is then applied to explain the nonlinearity observed in second harmonic generation (SHG) spectra within magnetic materials. Our analysis reveals that the dominant mechanism driving spectral displacement is the modulation of the magnon force constant caused by phonons, rather than changes in the temperature of thermal phonons. This insight is crucial for understanding and controlling the optical nonlinearity in magnetic dielectrics.

This work introduces a modified variant of the code-based cryptosystem developed by Loidreau. In this system, both the public and secret private keys are error codes; however, the overall security relies on the difficulty of transforming one set of error codes into another. The current approach employs a quadratic equation to generate the public key from the private key, creating a potential vulnerability exploitable via linear equation attacks. To counter this, the authors propose a novel construction that substitutes the traditional quadratic equation with a combination of a permutation and erasure operation. Furthermore, we introduce a novel method for transforming error codes featuring a sparse structure into those with a general sparse configuration, thereby broadening the scope of applicable code families for use as either public or private keys.

Recent studies indicate that extensive data scales and robust training architectures are critical for achieving state-of-the-art performance in recent years. However, these requirements often result in substantial computational costs and a reliance on massive corpora. To address this limitation, we introduce **Dict-BERT**, a novel pre-training architecture incorporating a dictionary module. This approach utilizes specialized terminology to enhance learning efficiency, thereby reducing dependence on large corpus volumes while competing with standard BERT. Experimental results demonstrate that Dict-BERT achieves performance comparable to standard BERT on MSRA and SQuAD benchmarks using only the MSRA-Wiki dataset. Additionally, we conducted comprehensive ablation studies to analyze the model's inner workings and explored various dictionary construction methods.

In this study, we analyze the asymptotic behavior of volumes associated with random minimal spanning acyclic structures and continuity diagrams of random complexes, extending previous work on minimal spanning trees. Our findings establish that, as the underlying point process intensity tends to infinity, the limiting volume for both minimal spanning acyclic and cycle-free structures is 1/3, whereas the volume limit for the tree structure remains 1/4. Additionally, we derive upper bounds on these volumes. We further demonstrate a sharp threshold: when the intensity exceeds a specific critical value, the limits of minimal spanning acyclic and cycle-free structures coincide with those of the tree, which is exclusive to the case of Poisson point processes. Finally, we prove a sharp threshold phenomenon wherein, below a critical intensity limit, the continuity diagrams of random complexes exhibit minimal spanning acyclic and cycle-free structures with volumes identical to those found in the Poisson case.

Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) is designed to harness the collective data of multiple parties for collaborative model training while keeping raw information local. This research investigates VFL's privacy guarantees, revealing that even under differential privacy (DP) constraints, the system remains vulnerable to pragmatic attacks. We introduce two novel methods: a data reconstruction attack that breaches differential privacy by exploiting the linear dependence among features, and a targeted model poisoning attack that undermines the utility of VFL outcomes. Our findings demonstrate that these attacks succeed across various scenarios, including differential privacy settings. Furthermore, we argue that VFL cannot fully secure data privacy in real-world applications because practical constraints often force the relaxation of formal differential privacy guarantees.

The Standard Model faces challenges from anomalies in $B$-meson decays, prompting investigations into the decay channel $B \to D' + X$, where $D'$ represents a baryon-antibaryon pair composed of dark matter. This study applies the QCD light-cone sum rules framework to determine the branching fraction for $B \to B' + X$ (where $B'$ is a dark baryon-antibaryon pair). The results indicate that the branching ratio is approximately $10^{-7}$, which is contingent upon the mass of the dark sector baryon.

This paper introduces the "Intelligent Urban Defense Game," a novel approach to social and socio-cyber-physical attacks that centers on tactical resource management for urban defense. Modeled as a multi-agent, non-cooperative game, the framework incorporates advanced machine learning techniques to optimize the allocation of resources. It specifically addresses two core issues: (1) dynamically locating high-risk zones by analyzing historical attack data, and (2) determining optimal resource distribution strategies to repel intrusions. To resolve these challenges, we developed a specialized algorithm leveraging a deep learning framework. Empirical results demonstrate that this method outperforms existing approaches in both risk prediction and resource administration. Furthermore, we created a dedicated simulator to evaluate the system, offering a practical platform for testing defensive tactics and defensive game AI within the context of intelligent city environments.

We investigate thermodynamic properties of "black star" solutions within Einstein's equations, specifically focusing on their phase transitions in an isolated system and when enclosed in a spherical cavity. These black star solutions, which emerge as a novel class alongside traditional black holes and thermodynamically distinct from them, arise as $d$-dimensional spherically symmetric configurations of mass $m$ and radius $r_c$ that satisfy a specific mass-radius relationship. This relationship features a minimum at a critical mass-radius ratio, corresponding to the most compact stable configuration. When situated in an isolated system, black stars exhibit a negative specific heat, rendering them thermodynamically unstable. Conversely, when confined within a spherical cavity, their thermodynamic behavior shifts significantly. This setup allows black stars to undergo Hawking--Page phase transitions, a phenomenon absent in standard black holes. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the upper branch of black stars possesses a phase transition that is a second-order transition, a behavior that differs from the first-order transitions typically associated with black hole transitions in similar contexts. These findings highlight the unique phase structure of black stars and their potential implications for understanding the nature of matter and energy in extreme gravitational fields.

This work introduces a novel group-based loss function for models processing data with label noise, treating it as an instance ranking problem. The approach constructs a bag around each mislabeled instance and optimizes the relative order of this contaminated example against its clean neighbors. The resulting loss function exhibits smoothness, convexity, and differentiability, and it can be efficiently optimized using a bag sampling strategy. The derived solution corresponds to a weighted variant of the Pairwise Loss function, where instance weights are determined by the specific configuration of each bag. Theoretically, this pairwise loss is proven to be non-increasing with respect to the group-based loss, establishing it as an upper bound. Furthermore, this upper bound provides a clear interpretation of the weighting applied to pairs in traditional pairwise loss. The final model, named BLPNet, is demonstrated to outperform existing methods on a newly created dataset featuring label noise, which was generated by randomly swapping labels from a clean image classifier.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have proven highly effective for learning representations within structured data, yet their performance often degrades when training relies on scarce labeled examples. To address this, pseudo-labeling has emerged as a promising strategy by generating and utilizing pseudo-labels to bolster GNN training. However, existing approaches typically depend on the pseudo-training model's confidence scores, which fail to account for the model's actual predictive accuracy. We introduce a novel pseudo-data tagging mechanism that identifies the most reliable pseudo-labels by incorporating the predictive performance of the GNN during training. We validate this approach across various pseudo-data generation techniques and tasks, demonstrating that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art solutions.

In the AWAKE Run 2 campaign, proton bunches are intended to drive beam-plasma instabilities within a solid target, prompting protons to emit betatron radiation. This study presents an initial quantitative analysis of that emission. The simulation framework integrates proton distribution generation, based on experimental parameters, with subsequent proton and photon energy spectra calculations. Results indicate that under Run 2 conditions, the generated photon flux is approximately $10^{10}$ photons per proton with an average energy of 100 keV. These findings are benchmarked against potential future scenarios, such as a proton-driven plasma wakefield acceleration context for the AWAKE Run 3 experiment.

Our approach employs the decision list paradigm, which enables a distributed implementation that guarantees differential privacy. We present a decision list algorithm grounded in the distance-based definition of differential privacy, offering a formal proof of its privacy compliance. This method is designed for distributed environments, with the distribution of training data across nodes determined by a distributional assumption. We provide a formal proof demonstrating that our distance-based DP decision list achieves $(\epsilon, \delta)$-differential privacy, where the parameters are defined as $\epsilon = \frac{\mu}{2} - \delta \cdot \frac{e^{2\mu} - 1}{2\delta \cdot e^{\mu}}$ and $\delta$ is a given probability level. Additionally, our DP decision list is capable of handling multi-class classification tasks. We also introduce a DP distributed decision tree algorithm, which is supported by a formal proof establishing its differential privacy. This study addresses regularized minimization problems involving Renyi entropy distances of orders $q \geq 1$, where the standard Euclidean quadratic distance is replaced. By employing techniques from Bregman analysis, we establish the existence of proximal gradient algorithms tailored to these generalized distances and ensure the non-expansivity of the corresponding proximal operators under conditions where the generating function is strongly convex. We further demonstrate that, for functions satisfying Lipschitz gradient conditions, the convergence rates of these algorithms mirror those of standard Euclidean proximal methods. The framework is extended to handle non-smooth data terms, yielding convergence results consistent with the proximal gradient case. We substantiate our theoretical findings through numerical experiments, illustrating the approach with examples from image denoising and clustering.

Chain Event Networks (ChENs) serve as a non-parametric extension of event chains, utilizing transition probabilities to model dynamic systems. Within a Bayesian context, ChENs allow for the estimation of unknown parameters, which can subsequently be used to analyze a system's predictive performance. This paper presents a framework for selecting ChEN models, specifically targeting the maximization of Bayesian Model Average (BMAB) predictions. The study evaluates the performance of proposed selection methods using both simulated data and real-world examples. The findings demonstrate that the new selection strategies yield superior predictive accuracy compared to standard approaches, which typically select models based on the Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) criterion.

We demonstrate that, under suitable conditions, these dynamics yield an asymptotic convergence to the $\alpha$-null space of a linear operator $A$, with the rate of convergence to the $\alpha$-minimal element governed by properties of the source kernel. This result holds for a broad spectrum of regularized dynamics, encompassing both damped inertial systems and the minimum principle of vanishing viscosity. This study examines the dynamics of a robot adhering to a vertical surface through suction cups, where the cups function as barriers that the robot must circumvent. We demonstrate that slight variations in the positions of these suction cups can result in abrupt and unpredictable changes in the robot's trajectory. Furthermore, we establish that the system's dynamics are chaotic, and this unpredictability persists even when the system operates within the standard regime of small parameters. Additionally, we identify a mechanism for abrupt behavioral flips: a stable periodic orbit can coexist with a chaotic one, meaning a minor alteration in initial conditions might cause the robot to switch between these two distinct behaviors.

We investigate the impact of disorder in kinetic-energy-driven superconductors, focusing on how superfluid density and zero-temperature microwave conductivity respond to doping and vary with energy gaps. Our analysis reveals that in the dilute limit of impurities, both quantities depend on the doping level in a manner dictated by the disorder's scattering classification, specifically whether it is short-range or long-range. Additionally, conductivity is governed by the distinction between particle-hole symmetric and asymmetric superconducting gaps. Given that kinetic-energy-based superconductivity is hypothesized to occur in the particle-hole asymmetric regime, our findings suggest that the corresponding experimental signatures in such materials are highly sensitive to the spatial profile of their disorder.

This paper examines a linearized average curvature framework that extends the study of crystalline motion. We provide a comprehensive review of this topic, covering the corresponding crystallized evolution process. We also present a detailed analysis of two specific methods for approximating average curvature: one utilizing a symmetric kernel and another employing a nonsymmetric kernel. Additionally, we derive a novel approximation method based on a symmetric kernel and demonstrate its validity by establishing the convergence of this discrete scheme to a solution of a nonlocal variational flow. Finally, we analyze the behavior of this approach in the local setting, where it coincides with mean curvature motion, and establish proof of both discrete and continuous convergence.

Plants serve as vital resources for human survival, offering both food and raw materials for various products. While humans have historically shaped plant growth for both utility and aesthetics, the precise methods for sculpting plants for specific functional outputs remain largely unexplored. This paper introduces GrowSpace, the inaugural interactive platform designed to investigate plant modification for enhanced performance. Within this space, users can curate a starting plant, apply various editing tools, and assess the resulting yield. The paper details the underlying architecture of GrowSpace and presents preliminary findings from a pilot study that offers foundational insights into user behaviors and expert knowledge regarding plant sculpting.

This paper demonstrates that the self-dual local geometry governing the chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution (SLE$_\kappa$) for $2 < \kappa < 4$ is governed by trivalent trees where every vertex is connected via quantum disks. Specifically, the conformal structure on these quantum disks arises from an appropriately tuned Truncated SLE$_\kappa$ cycle—a random path that commences and concludes at $0$ and $1$ within the domain $[0,1]$ with $D$ and moves toward $D$, where $D$ represents the upper half-plane equipped with the Brownian motion-derived Liouville quantum field metric. By analyzing this cycle, the authors establish a correspondence between its segments and the distinct local geometries observed at trivalent tree nodes. The derivation relies on two main components: a newly constructed Liouville correlation function involving Brownian motion and a recent finding by Coublange, Gwynne, Miller, and Qian concerning the boundary length of quantum $D$-disks.

This study examines the contributions of high-spin nucleon resonances to $K\Lambda$ and $K\sum$ photoproduction, utilizing a dynamical model that incorporates the $s$-, $d$-, and $f$-wave resonances spanning from 1.5 to 2.2 GeV. Our findings indicate that these high-spin states significantly influence the angular distributions, particularly in the forward region, and affect the overall magnitude of the cross sections. To address this, we propose a new set of isospin-symmetric, modified Breit-Wigner amplitudes to better align with experimental data. This adjustment involves scaling the Breit-Wigner magnitude by the square root of the branching fractions for the respective $K\Lambda$ and $K\sum$ decay channels. This method successfully accounts for the observed discrepancies between standard $s$-, $d$-, and $f$-wave amplitudes and the measured experimental results.

This paper details the application of the OpenCV toolset to pre-treat images from the MORPH-II database. As one of the world's largest repositories of color faces, the MORPH-II set comprises 145,500 color images of 128x128 pixels from 80,187 individuals, with a mean age of 50 years. Because the set is heavily weighted toward male subjects, it is particularly valuable for advancing facial recognition research. The primary objective of this study is to enhance the accuracy of facial recognition systems by applying OpenCV to improve image quality. The authors evaluated various preprocessing techniques, including contrast enhancement, color-to-grayscale conversion, and image rescaling. The findings indicate that the most significant gains in recognition accuracy stem from converting to grayscale and applying contrast enhancement.

We demonstrate that a curvaton decaying into the channel $\phi \to 2B$, where $\phi$ represents the curvaton and $B$ denotes a black hole, can successfully generate the primordial power spectrum. This mechanism is viable because the curvaton undergoes decay into black holes within its Hubble horizon, a process occurring shortly after its reheating phase. This phenomenon is applicable to both de Sitter and inflationary backgrounds. The resulting black hole population subsequently evaporates via Hawking radiation, thereby producing the primordial perturbation spectrum.

This study introduces a latent variable approach designed to identify the sequence of courses that best supports students in reaching their selected major. We train a latent variable model on historical data from the University of Minnesota, evaluating its performance through various metrics. The results indicate that courses predicted by our model align closely with those actually taken by students, particularly within the same major. Additionally, the model successfully uncovers hidden course groups that exhibit distinct patterns of enrollment.

This study introduces a novel differential framework for governing the aggregation of autonomous vehicle platoons, where each unit engages in a linked contest with its neighbor. The proposed system is formulated as a set of coupled ordinary differential equations, and its dynamic behavior is analyzed through both theoretical derivation and numerical simulations. The work further explores the convergence properties of these equations, and under specific conditions, it examines their equilibrium states, stability, and long-term behavior. The authors also investigate the impact of various parameters on system dynamics, and discuss potential applications in real-world scenarios.

This study addresses interaction effects within logistic regression. We introduce a novel framework for identifying interaction variables, reinterpreting traditional methods under this new perspective. By defining interaction as the discrepancy between the specific effect of a variable within a subset and its overall marginal effect, we establish a general model that encompasses both continuous and categorical variables. This formulation reveals that the sign of the interaction is determined by the distance between the subgroup's overall effect and zero, while the magnitude depends on the size of this distance as well as the difference between the original and the subgroup's respective overall effects. We leverage this model to develop a new strategy for selecting variables involved in interactions. Furthermore, through a combination of theoretical analysis and empirical testing, we demonstrate that this proposed method offers superior statistical performance.

Headlines are concise, engaging summaries that frequently appear alongside news articles. While existing research has primarily concentrated on generating headlines from raw text, this work addresses the inverse challenge: automatically creating concise headlines from completed articles. We evaluate this by creating a new dataset comprising over 10,000 news pairs consisting of both the original articles and their corresponding headlines. We then apply state-of-the-art Transformer models to tackle this task, with results indicating that such a system can generate headline-quality outputs indistinguishable from human writing.

We investigate chiral magnetism within spin-1/2 systems exhibiting both polycrystalline and amorphous characteristics. By employing Monte Carlo simulations to explore the phase diagrams of these configurations, we identify a distinctive chiral spin fluid phase situated between a conventional helical order and an incommensurate state. Notably, this unique phase persists across a broad range of temperatures and occurs even in highly disordered environments, underscoring the robustness of chiral magnetism. Additionally, we examine the phase diagram of the J1-J2 model in polycrystalline setups, confirming the coexistence of the previously identified polycrystalline ferromagnetic and helical phases alongside this new chiral spin fluid.

Radio interferometers are essential for studying the cosmos, yet their capabilities are constrained by imperfect phase and amplitude measurements. To address this, calibration techniques are employed to derive phase and amplitude corrections that restore interferometric fidelity. While effective methods like self-calibration and beamforming exist, they are computationally prohibitive for large-scale instruments, typically requiring $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ operations where $N$ denotes the number of antennas. We introduce a novel algorithm grounded in the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) capable of reducing computational complexity to $\mathcal{O}(N\log{N})$. This approach is applicable to interferometers arranged on a regular grid, such as those utilizing the Delay/Beamforming technique. We validate the method's performance and computational efficiency using data from the Square Kilometre Array Pre-feasibility Study (SKA-PFS) configuration.

This study introduces a new approach to portfolio diversification by training an autoencoder conditional generative adversarial network (AEcGAN) to generate multiple similar yet distinct market trajectories. The resulting synthetic paths serve to evaluate the performance of diversification strategies. We specifically investigate the potential of diversification into cryptocurrencies, utilizing the AEcGAN framework to create multiple future price sequences for both Bitcoin and Ethereum. The analysis reveals that diversifying into these assets enhances returns while reducing risk compared to an investment solely in gold. Furthermore, we examine the impact of transaction costs on these strategies, observing that while such costs reduce overall performance, the advantage of diversification into cryptocurrencies and through gold remains consistent.

This work presents the calculation of the polarized three-loop matrix component $A_{gq}(N)$ for the gluon-to-quark transition, which appears in the variable flavor number scheme (VFNS) when transforming to the Mellin conjugate space. This contribution is necessary for determining the one-loop ($O(\alpha_s)$) VFNS gluon and quark distributions, $g(x)$ and $q_i(x)$, and the corresponding Mellin moments. The derived $A_{gq}(N)$ results are provided up to terms of $1/N$ and $1/N^2$.

This study introduces a Bayesian neural network to classify the LAT catalog of the Fermi-LAT database, specifically targeting active galactic nuclei (AGN) and distinguishing between Seyfert 1 and blazar subtypes. We train the network using a dataset comprising 1,000 blazars, 1,000 Seyfert 1 galaxies, and 1,000 randomly selected galaxies from the catalog. Our approach incorporates five features: the gamma-ray flux, the ratio of X-ray to gamma-ray flux, and the redshift, along with two Bayesian uncertainty metrics. We evaluate the network's performance through testing on an independent dataset of 3,000 catalog entries and by analyzing prediction errors on the training data. The results indicate that the model achieves 99.9% accuracy in identifying blazars, 99.9% for Seyfert 1s, and 99.9% for other galaxies. Notably, the inclusion of Bayesian uncertainty measures is critical for classification success.

We demonstrate that the eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix resulting from the tensor union consist of the combined spectra of the constituent hypergraphs, alongside additional terms derived from the ranks and sizes of those hypergraphs.
