We introduce a comprehensive framework for constructing scattering amplitudes in general relativistic settings, grounded in the principles of Lorentz invariance and translational invariance. This approach enables the derivation of the Einstein field equations as well as scalar field equations within a curved spacetime context via a unified perspective. Furthermore, our theory elucidates the significance of the Schwarzian derivative in gravity and delineates the boundaries of validity for the post-Newtonian approximation.

This study investigates the stabilization of the local-in-time strong solutions to the 3D and 4D Navier-Stokes equations (n=3 or 4) in critical $L^q$-based Sobolev and Besov spaces through a finite-dimensional, internally located state feedback control. Building upon the methodology of Cui and Wang (2017), we establish that uniform stabilization is feasible for the regulated system. Furthermore, we demonstrate that any finite-dimensional version of this specific feedback control achieves the same uniform stabilization effect. These theoretical findings are substantiated by numerical simulations.

We introduce LitMind, a comprehensive open-source online dictionary dedicated to the Classical and Early Medieval Chinese literary tradition. It features freely accessible entries for over 10,000 significant terms, each supported by more than 100 classical citations. This resource was developed to facilitate scholarly research and education by offering rich contextual examples for core vocabulary. Future iterations will expand support to Classical and Early Medieval Latin and Sogdian.

Explainable recommendation systems (RS) are essential for user trust, yet they must also ensure that explanations align with actual predictions. This study evaluates common LIME-RS methods against two stability and one compliance requirement. Using established recommendation benchmarks, we demonstrate that these approaches fail to consistently meet these criteria, particularly when multiple valid LIME-RS outputs exist for a single query. To address this, we introduce a new LIME-RS method that satisfies all three requirements and shows improved consistency compared to existing models.

This study investigates the pinning of the Fermi level at the valence band edge in near-surface InAs quantum wells within Si, a phenomenon driven by the introduction of deep acceptor states via Si-induced defects. To mitigate this pinning effect, we have engineered a Si buffer layer doped with boron. Experimental results indicate that employing this optimized buffer layer successfully eliminates the valence band edge Fermi level pinning in InAs quantum wells deposited on the new substrate.

Resilient learning addresses the challenge of training neural networks when data is contaminated with noise. This work provides a theoretical examination of when regional queries—where model parameters are estimated using local subsamples rather than the entire dataset—are advantageous for achieving resilience. We demonstrate that regional queries yield superior resilience performance under two specific conditions: (1) when the true data distribution is well-represented across all subsamples, and (2) when the majority of regional queries remain free from noise. Furthermore, we establish that regional queries can attain better empirical risk than the standard empirical risk minimization approach in certain scenarios. These findings are supported by a generalized concept of "well-covered" subsets, which is both theoretically grounded and practically applicable to real-world datasets.

This study introduces a novel rapid algorithm for approximating optimal transport costs between discrete measures, representing the subsequent development of the Rapid Sinkhorn algorithm proposed by Perrin et al. (2021). While Rapid Sinkhorn accelerates convergence for problems where traditional methods are prohibitively slow, Rapid OTN retains the linear time complexity ($O(n)$) per iteration required for precise solutions, enabling its application to a broader spectrum of problems. The convergence rate of this new algorithm is analyzed for a specific case: the computation of optimal transport between two triangular arrays in one dimension. This configuration is a critical step in calculating the Fréchet–Hausdorff distance between triangular arrays, a metric that serves as a proxy for the Wasserstein distance in machine learning and computer vision contexts. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the convergence speed of our algorithm in this one-dimensional scenario is independent of the number of iterations, contingent solely on the initial step size.

This study presents the most comprehensive investigation of UV emissions from the young, active M dwarf AU Mic, utilizing data from the IUE satellite and the Hubble Space Telescope's Cosmic Origins Spectrograph (HST/COS). The analysis includes 11 far-UV (FUV) observations: five capturing the star in a quiescent state and six during significant flares. These observations were analyzed to determine the spectral energy distribution (SED) of AU Mic and to assess its chromospheric and coronal activity. The derived SEDs for both active and quiescent states indicate that AU Mic possesses a hot corona extending to temperatures of at least 1 MK, alongside chromospheric activity that is notably stronger than typical for low-mass main-sequence stars. Furthermore, the study examines the impact of this enhanced activity on the habitability of its close-orbiting planets, AU Mic b and c. We find that chromospheric emissions likely exert a more significant influence on the atmospheric stability of these planets than X-ray radiation. Finally, we explore the mechanisms by which FUV and UV radiation drive atmospheric loss, concluding that the planets' extended atmospheres are highly susceptible to photoevaporation driven by the star's intense activity.

We investigate the motion of a particle traveling through a resistive medium characterized by random binary states and random switching dynamics. When the particle undergoes random transitions between states, the system's behavior is governed by a generalized master equation. In the specific limit where transition rates between states are high, the dynamics are described by a generalized Fokker-Planck equation. For a chosen initial state distribution, the asymptotic evolution of this equation can be captured by a modified Boltzmann equation. Furthermore, the friction force experienced by a single particle within this environment is derived from solutions to this equation.

In the field of pattern recognition, the nearest neighbor classifier is renowned for its simplicity and effectiveness, particularly when dealing with numerical data. However, this approach often falters when faced with imbalanced datasets, where the distribution of class frequencies is unequal. This paper introduces a statistical technique designed to adjust numerical features in such datasets, thereby enhancing classification accuracy. By applying this proposed method, we successfully tested it against two well-known benchmarks—the Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer dataset and the Wisconsin Prostate Diagnostic dataset—finding that it outperforms several established techniques.

We introduce an updated catalog of 1,000 ultra-bright quasar candidates identified by the SkyMapper survey, achieved by merging data from 100 observing sessions with a $u$-band magnitude limit of 14.5. By cross-referencing this list with existing databases, we isolated 162 objects with no prior high-luminosity counterparts. Spectroscopic analysis of 110 of these new discoveries revealed 107 quasar candidates, with 10 confirmed as quasars. These findings establish the most comprehensive spectroscopic catalog of luminous quasars ($M_U < -25.5$) assembled to date. We identified one confirmed quasar at $z=7.05$ and another at $z=6.82$, both of which are newly reported. Additionally, we detected a record number of 11 quasars at redshifts exceeding 6.5, with a luminosity of $M_U < -27.5$, suggesting a potential peak in the luminosity function at these extreme values. We also identified 11 quasar candidates with redshifts greater than 6.5 that possess the highest luminosities known to date, with $M_U > -29.5$. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the evolution of quasars and the broader context of black hole growth.

The ability to detect individual charge tunneling events within superconducting islands is a vital prerequisite for advancing superconducting quantum circuits. In this study, we present a comprehensive analysis of a gate-tunneling setup where a superconducting domain coexists with a quantum point contact. By employing a nearby gate electrode, we successfully identify discrete tunneling occurrences. Our findings reveal that the signal from these events exhibits non-monotonic behavior with respect to gate voltage, a feature attributed to the interplay between the superconducting region and the point defect. These results offer a detailed exploration of charge transport in superconductors coupled with localized defects, providing essential insights for the evolution of superconducting-based quantum technologies.

Eternal views serve as a valuable visual format for historical sites, museums, and landscapes, yet their creation from a single new 360-degree image often relies on labor-intensive manual editing. This paper introduces "DiffDreamer," an automated system that generates eternal views from single 360-degree images using conditional diffusion models. Evidenced by our results from the HistoDreamer challenge, this approach achieves superior performance over all existing methods. Furthermore, we developed an open-source model trained on historical data that demonstrates impressive capabilities in generating realistic outcomes.

This work addresses the challenge of forecasting and managing complex networked systems, such as the spread of infectious diseases, by utilizing solely the network's topology. We introduce a new framework capable of predicting the future dynamics of Networked SIS (Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible) models. Our approach involves two primary stages: first, identifying the Networked SIS model's parameters by leveraging a recently developed, data-driven neural network architecture; second, employing these inferred parameters to forecast system evolution and determine the necessary control measures to regulate the networked process. Notably, this methodology requires only knowledge of the network's structure and a minimal dataset, making it highly applicable to various networked systems. We validate our framework through extensive simulations on both synthetic and real-world networks, demonstrating its effectiveness in both prediction and regulation.

This study examines the instability of a liquid layer coating a cylindrical fiber, focusing on how surface slip influences rupture. We compare an analytical framework, which models the system as an infinite Rayleigh-Plateau instability, against a spectral method that provides the rigorous stability analysis for finite fibers. The results indicate that slip significantly delays the onset of breakup. Furthermore, we identify an intermediate range of slip magnitudes where the instability growth rate aligns with the theoretical prediction, a phenomenon that matches observations of water dripping from a cord suspended in air.

We demonstrate that the newly introduced hunter-saxton formula, which expresses the $S^1$-equivalence between the Lipschitz norms on the geodesic spaces of two Riemannian metrics, ensures the preservation of Hunter-Saxton well-posedness. This framework, which utilizes a novel metric to resolve long-standing issues in original hunter-saxton formulation, is detailed in our previous work (arXiv:2003.09076). Using this metric's specific properties, we establish that the space of Hunter-Saxton formula is locally compact and complete, ensuring the existence of unique local solutions to the geodesic equation. This approach also enables us to establish the existence of global solutions for initial data with sufficiently small $S^1$-equivalent Sobolev norms.

This study introduces a robotic framework designed to automate the scoliosis ultrasound workflow, a process currently hampered by the need for repeated scans due to inconsistent manual probe positioning. The system integrates a robotic arm with an ultrasound transducer to generate spinal images for curvature assessment. We present a new automated segmentation technique that contrasts with existing methods by eliminating the computationally expensive and unreliable reliance on spine-specific anatomical landmarks. Instead, our approach utilizes a deep learning model trained on manually scanned data to predict scoliosis metrics directly from the imagery. Experimental results indicate that the automated segmentation successfully replicates human expert measurements with a correlation coefficient of 0.96, demonstrating that the proposed robotics platform offers a viable, high-precision solution for automating scoliosis evaluation.

This study introduces a novel technique for determining the speech duration of unseen segments by integrating a median-based approach with synthetic waveform generation. We evaluate this method on a standard dataset, comparing it against two non-statistical and two statistical prediction models. Results indicate our approach achieves superior accuracy over all compared statistical and non-statistical methods. We attribute this success to the absence of any statistical assumptions or training data requirements, which allows the system to remain invariant to diverse speech characteristics, including speaker identity, linguistic content, and recording conditions.

This study introduces a new model designed to detect hate speech, which integrates the strengths of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs). We applied this architecture to the dataset from the 2019 Kagame Challenge on Hate Speech and Inclusive AI. Our approach features a dual-stream design: the initial layer focuses on identifying toxic content, while the subsequent layer targets specifically hateful instances. Experimental results demonstrate that this method surpasses existing solutions on the specified hate speech detection task.

This research addresses the challenge of feature exchanging within Multi-Instance Multi-Output (MIMO) learning, a method designed to handle scenarios with multiple similar input instances and multiple distinct output targets. We introduce a novel feature exchanging mechanism that not only generates a consolidated set of input instances but also creates multiple output representations, each dedicated to a specific output label. By integrating this approach with the Multi-Instance Multi-Output (MIMO) framework, we formulate a corresponding learning algorithm. Experimental results indicate that our method achieves superior performance compared to several existing techniques.

This paper offers a survey of public collections featuring images of historical manuscripts, which are available through digital archives. We provide an overview of the various criteria used in these datasets to describe the content and physical traits of the manuscripts. Furthermore, we examine how these resources are employed in the context of research and applications.

This study details the implementation of a flatness-based controller for regulating the position of an industrial robot arm through the secondary sensing of its drive motor's rotational speed. In this adaptive approach, a nonlinear model model is estimated online using speed data collected from a secondary sensor, such as an encoder. Once updated, the controller calculates the necessary torques to track a desired trajectory. The effectiveness of this real-time model identification strategy is validated via experimental results.

This paper introduces a multiple-state model (MMLE) designed to evaluate multidimensional time-to-event data and life-course health pathways, specifically for patients with myocardial infarction. The MMLE approach extends the classic Cox model by incorporating multiple states, thereby accommodating various transitions between them. By integrating multidimensional time-to-event data and life-course health pathways, the MMLE framework offers a comprehensive strategy for analyzing complex patient trajectories. It is a promising method for investigating the intricate interplay between multiple risk factors and multidimensional health outcomes. The study applies this model to real-world data from patients with acute myocardial infarction, examining the associations between risk factors and multiple health pathways. The results indicate that the MMLE model effectively captures these intricate relationships, providing valuable insights into the disease progression and potential interventions for patients with acute myocardial infarction.

Molecular dynamics simulations frequently rely on models that incorporate molecular continuum representations of surrounding bulk environments. However, evaluating these continua via direct atomistic atomistics is computationally prohibitive. To address this, we introduce an efficient and precise quadrature method for molecular continuum evaluation. This approach utilizes a fixed set of sites and associated weights derived from rigorous numerical integration techniques originally designed for the electrostatic continuum. The method's robustness is validated against diverse molecular systems, including DNA, proteins, and small molecules, demonstrating strong agreement with rigorous analytical benchmarks.

The metric dimension of a graph $G$ refers to the smallest cardinality of a vertex subset $S$ where every vertex outside $S$ possesses a unique projection onto $S$ based on shortest-path distances. This paper investigates the parameterization problem for metric dimension, leveraging recent findings that establish metric dimension as W[1]-hard when parameterized by treewidth, and further proving its W[1]-hardness via several additional structural parameters, including feedback vertex number, branchwidth, pathwidth, rankwidth, and the maximum degree of a clique. In response, we demonstrate that a fixed-parameter algorithm exists for metric dimension using feedback vertex group size as a parameter, provided the group size is small. This result relies on constructing an algorithm that combines an existing kernelization method with an exponential-time solver. Additionally, we show the problem remains solvable in polynomial time when the parameter corresponds to the group size of a specific subset of vertices, where that subset is provided as part of the input instance.

This results in a day-to-day pattern of intense downpours, which are most intense near the equator and diminish toward the poles. We introduce twistor-constructive solutions to four-dimensional self-dual Yang-Mills theory across arbitrary complex Lie groups and generalize these findings to an infinite family of non-Abelian self-dual Yang-Mills models featuring elevated spin parameters ($\lambda$). In each case, the resulting space of solutions exhibits a twistor-theoretic origin. Furthermore, these twistor-realizations admit interpretations as infinite-dimensional generalizations of the Dorey-Balog twists previously identified in non-Abelian Taub-Nahle and other solitonic configurations. A key component of our approach involves extending the concept of a Penzias line to a new framework known as $\lambda$-twistor space, where we define a generalized boundary condition for connection matrices that ensures their self-duality.

This study addresses the challenge of noisy label categorization in deep learning for medical image analysis. While deep neural networks have proven effective across numerous image analysis tasks, performance in this specific domain is often constrained by imperfect labels. To mitigate this, we introduce a self-contained, self-service label correction mechanism that operates independently of data augmentation, data selection techniques, or weak-supervision learning strategies. The method applies Bayesian analytics to deep neural networks to infer the probability of correct classification for training samples. These estimated correction probabilities are then integrated with a label restoration algorithm to refine the initial noisy annotations. Experimental results across three datasets spanning diverse image analysis tasks indicate that this approach consistently enhances data quality and yields robust model performance.

We have previously established a general theorem regarding the bounds of interpolation operators acting on continuous functions within a metric space. In this paper, we employ that theorem to derive an upper limit for the norm of the interpolation operator based on the position of its interpolation nodes.

Graphs and their polynomials have been extensively studied in mathematics and computer science. In this paper, we examine the relationship between a graph's random walk transition likelihood matrix and a specific polynomial. To this end, we introduce a novel random walk model where the likelihood matrix entry $L_{ij}$ represents the probability of moving from vertex $i$ to vertex $j$ if a direct edge exists, or is zero otherwise. This matrix is constructed as the diagonal of a specific polynomial derived from the graph's vertex and edge structures. Our findings include the derivation of the degree of this featured polynomial and the identification of the rank of the likelihood matrix. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the likelihood matrix and the graph's Laplacian matrix. Finally, we propose a dynamic model that tracks the evolution of random walk probabilities over time.

We introduce a new class of definitions called "timed definitions" to HOL, which are intended to support the systematic development of complex systems. These definitions incorporate a timing dimension that tracks changes in term values over time, facilitating the formal verification of properties related to value evolution. This formalism allows for the straightforward introduction of continuous state variations and the direct reasoning regarding temporal value fluctuations. We have implemented a prototype in HOL that features an definitions mechanism capable of handling both static and temporal values as well as supporting both equational and non-equinal forms of definition.

This study introduces a turbulence modeling approach that integrates turbulence closure systems with turbulence structure equations. The model is constructed using the Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) equations augmented by an additional transport equation for the turbulent kinetic energy dissipation rate, $\epsilon$. A key feature of the proposed framework is its utilization of the instantaneous logarithmic velocity profile to establish a relationship between $\epsilon$ and the friction velocity, $u_\tau$. This relationship allows the instantaneous boundary $u_\tau$ to be solved alongside mean velocity and pressure within the domain. The resulting four-variable system accurately captures complex flows, including those with separated regions, and produces high-quality results for both wall-bounded turbulence and wall-perpendicular pressure gradients.

This study examines $Q$-ball solitons within a nonlinear generalization of the infant Skyrme model, characterized by its ability to support self-dual vortex solutions. While these solitons exhibit a minimum in their energy per baryonic number at quanta of $Q=2$, corresponding to vortex loops, we identify a specific parameter regime where the model yields $Q=1$ self-dual vortex rings.

The Hofstadter map is a theoretical model that describes the energy spectrum of a particle within a periodic potential subjected to a strong external magnetic field. This study introduces a novel class of materials: Weyl semimetals exhibiting time-reversal violation operating in the Hofstadter regime. This category is characterized by a lattice with broken time-reversal symmetry, where a strong magnetic field is commensurate with the underlying lattice periodicity. This specific configuration generates a complex spectrum of electronic states, and we demonstrate that the spectrum of a time-reversal-violating Hofstadter semimagnet features a set of Dirac points. These Dirac points are distinguished by their high sensitivity to magnetic flux, magnetic field intensity, and the specific lattice potential. Furthermore, the system is predicted to exhibit a unique combination of properties, including a quantized Hall effect, a significant anomalous Hall effect, and a Hofstadter-type surface state. These characteristics suggest that such a material could serve as a robust platform for investigating topological phenomena and potential applications in quantum technologies.

Plasmonic optical antennas are renowned for their ability to interact with light at the nanoscale, yet losses inherent to plasmonics often limit their ability to emit radiation effectively. In response, this study proposes a novel hybrid dielectric-plasmonic nanoantenna structure designed to overcome these drawbacks. The configuration features a plasmonic bowtie antenna situated atop a one-dimensional photonic crystal slab. Theoretical analysis indicates that this architecture facilitates highly efficient, luminous, and unidirectional light emission. Specifically, the plasmonic bowtie acts as a nanoantenna to capture incident waves, while the underlying one-dimensional photonic crystal slab functions as a resonator. Under normal incidence, the hybrid structure exhibits a pronounced and unidirectional Fano resonance. Furthermore, the plasmonic bowtie antenna generates a substantial magnetic dipole moment that couples with a weaker electric dipole moment. This coupling yields a remarkably high quality factor (Q) for the hybrid nanoantenna, enabling superior light-matter interaction. Additionally, the bowtie's anisotropic radiation pattern allows for the separation of incident and reflected beams, thereby achieving a highly efficient and direction-specific scattering response.

In 2017, T. C. Halsey and colleagues proposed the concept of "shielding" to explain the anomalous rheological behaviors exhibited by dense granular flows. This work introduces a novel experimental approach designed to validate the shielding theory by investigating the anisotropic normal stresses that emerge within granular substances under shear. Normal stress anisotropy is assessed through the use of a newly developed rheometer featuring a four-post configuration, which allows for independent shear and normal stress measurements along both the expansion and contraction principal axes. Experimental outcomes are then contrasted with numerical simulations of a two-dimensional binary granular system subjected to identical shear and normal stresses. The strong agreement between the empirical data and simulation results confirms that the proposed experimental methodology effectively supports Halsey's shielding theory regarding granular material dynamics.

Using first-principles calculations, we investigate the electronic and magnetic properties of silicon monolayer decorated with manganese atoms placed on a hexagonal boron nitride substrate. Our results show that the silicene-substrate interaction is weakly physisorptive, allowing the substrate to effectively induce large band splitting in the spin-polarized states of the Manganese-decorated system. Additionally, the magnetic moments of the Manganese atom are significantly modified by both the silicon layer and the boron nitride substrate. Ultimately, our study confirms the feasibility of generating large, tunable spin-polarized currents through the combination of 2D materials and transition metal adsorbates.

Sgr A East is a supernova remnant situated in the Galactic Center, whose origin remains uncertain, with debates focusing on whether it resulted from the explosion of a massive star or the merger of a compact object. By analyzing the spatial distribution of emission from the remnant, we determine that the explosion likely occurred within the dense core of the nuclear star cluster. This finding supports the hypothesis that Sgr A East was triggered by the merger of a compact object, specifically a white dwarf, rather than core-collapse of a massive star.

In the field of text classification, Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) have become a standard approach for handling the increasing volume of unstructured data. However, ANN models are prone to overfitting, particularly when dealing with small datasets. To mitigate this issue, various strategies have been developed to enhance the robustness of these models. One such method is Artificial Neural Network-based Data Augmentation (ANNA), which involves generating synthetic samples to enrich training data. This study evaluates ANNA's effectiveness in a multi-category text classification task by benchmarking it against other popular overfitting reduction techniques, including SMOTE, Random Over-Sampling, and a new approach called Balanced Bagging. The research analyzes the impact of overfitting reduction on classification performance by measuring accuracy across different overfitting levels.

This study investigates the interconnected dynamics between COVID-19 coverage in U.S. regional news outlets and the associated public response, specifically examining how such coverage influences viewership, digital engagement, and audience behavior. Utilizing a dataset of 100,000 news stories alongside viewership and digital data from March to July 2020, the research employs regression models to analyze the impact of news content on audience metrics. The findings reveal a strong positive correlation between the extent of COVID-19 news coverage and audience size, indicating that both viewership and digital engagement expand as coverage intensifies. Notably, regression results show that viewership tends to peak in markets heavily exposed to the pandemic, whereas digital engagement remains relatively constant regardless of infection rates. Furthermore, the study identifies a "market effect," where regional news consumption is larger in areas with broader regional market reach. Ultimately, the research underscores the critical role of media in disseminating COVID-19 information and highlights how news coverage significantly shapes audience dynamics in both online and traditional formats.

The interaction of angular-dependent multipole sources with targets is efficiently computed using the Rapid Multipole Technique (RMT). However, during a multipole-to-local multipole (MLLP) transformation, a fixed truncation of angular moments can lead to data loss. We present an improved, angular-consistent MLLP approach designed to preserve angular momentum. We also examine the relationship between this new method and the multipole-to-multipoles (MTM) transformation, ultimately applying the angle-consistent MLLP method to scattering calculations. We conclude that this approach significantly enhances the convergence rate for targets of a fixed complexity.

This study examines the transmission of polarization from incident to scattered protons within elastic electron-proton interactions. By analyzing the asymptotic behavior of the relevant polarization asymmetries and spin-alignment parameters, we demonstrate that the proton's intrinsic convection of spin arises primarily from its anomalous magnetic moment. Furthermore, we establish that the magnitude of these effects scales with the ratio of the anomalous magnetic moment to the total proton spin.

This paper presents a novel method for enhancing data utility in scenarios involving modular expert architectures. We demonstrate that our approach enables agents to acquire tasks more efficiently by leveraging a group of parametric specialists, each trained on distinct subsets of data. Furthermore, we outline a strategy for automatically determining the quantity of experts required to perform a specific task effectively. Extensive evaluations across various task complexities—from simpler benchmarks to challenging reasoning tasks—using state-of-the-art language models, validate that our data augmentation technique results in a substantial improvement in sample efficiency.

The study relies on 139 fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity gathered from the Center for Energy for Mass (CEFF) facility. The results are based on the detection of two Higgs bosons in the decay mode of four leptons and two photons. The findings are compared with theoretical predictions from the Standard Model. The results show that the cross-section of production is consistent with the Standard Model. The results are also presented in terms of signal strength, which is a measure of the cross-section of production divided by the Standard Model prediction. Spin masers are unique among laser counterparts as they operate at quantum limits where decoherence and thermal noise dominate their behavior. We introduce a method to implement spin maser logic using an alkaline gas, where the qubit states consist of an alkali atom's ground-state spin and one photon. Our framework achieves fully digital control of this quantum logic through precisely timed, off-resonant photon pulses. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a digital implementation offers superior resilience to photon dephasing and photon loss compared to its analog counterpart.

We demonstrate that a dark matter scenario featuring an evolving neutralino relic density aligns with current cosmological observations. This scenario requires the neutralino to be nearly self-interacting and undergo late-time decay into a dark sector particle. As a consequence, the dark sector acts as a vacuum energy component, and the neutralino itself constitutes dark matter. The predicted gamma-ray spectral signature from the decay process into a photon and a dark sector particle is examined, and the study concludes that such signals could potentially be detectable by the Fermi Large Area Telescope.

Graph theory has recently seen a surge in the study of graph genus, driven by applications in network design and the development of new genus estimation techniques. Thick graphs, defined as graphs where edges are replaced by edge-disjoint simple cycles, are a specific focus of this work. We demonstrate that the genus can be estimated in polynomial time for this class, yielding a genus upper bound that is asymptotically tight. Furthermore, we introduce a specific subclass known as thickenings of multigraphs, where thickened edges are cycle-replaced simple thickener graphs. In this scenario, we show that genuse estimation is achievable in linear time, with an asymptonicaly tighnt genuse upper bound. Our findings build upon foundational insights from Diestel and Thiele, who established the graph theoretic context, and extend the work of Babel and Urrutia, who worked on related classes of graphs.

We introduce and analyze a randomized Newton method for convex optimization with linear constraints designed for distributed environments. Our approach operates by having each agent in a network independently manage a subset of equality and a subset of convex objective functions. Agents communicate exclusively with immediate neighbors to iteratively determine feasible solutions. We establish convergence rates for both the feasible objective values and the overall optimality gap. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the method remains robust against noise in the subgradient estimates of the equality constraints. Our findings indicate that the randomized technique offers communication and computational efficiencies, as well as reduced latencies, when compared to established algorithms.

Time projection chambers (TPCs) are widely used for detecting nuclear recoils from dark matter interactions. However, these signals are challenging to identify amidst overwhelming backgrounds from cosmic rays and neutrinos. To address this, this study introduces and evaluates three new observables that enhance recoil discrimination: (1) the time difference between a chamber cell's charge onset and its peak, (2) the charge diffusion magnitude, and (3) drift distance. Validating these measurables using data from a $^3$He-based TPC, the research demonstrates a significant improvement in detection efficiency while maintaining background rejection rates. Specifically, for a fixed number of retained background events, nuclear detection efficiency can be boosted by 30% to 50% compared to standard identification methods.

Intelligent systems are increasingly employed to automate critical decisions in high-stakes fields like healthcare and justice, raising significant concerns regarding the fairness of these automations. A primary challenge is that standard evaluation practices, which often rely on aggregate metrics like error rates, can obscure biases affecting specific demographic groups. To address this, we introduce a framework for contextualized evaluation that considers real-world decision-making scenarios. This approach utilizes intelligent choices—specialized models designed to determine the most appropriate method for assessing a system's equity within a particular context. By selecting an optimal evaluation strategy based on the specific risks and nature of the domain, these methods ensure a more precise and meaningful analysis of algorithmic fairness.

This document details the findings from the Out-of-Lexicon Challenge, an evaluation where models must predict part-of-speech (POS) tags for inputs containing only previously unseen forms. The study highlights the difficulty of relying solely on lexical frequency, noting that many inflectional patterns are irregular. We detail the experimental design, baseline approaches, and the performance of the top three entries, concluding that the task remains challenging for current methods.

We analyze Gaussian stochastic fields to model the probabilistic emergence of low-dimensional manifolds, presenting field-based measures of curvature and geodesics for their identification. These tools enable the direct mapping of curvature-driven trajectories and other manifold features within the stochastic fields themselves, a method applied to two specific cases: a Gelfand-Zhang diffusion process and a real-space renormalization group field.

This study introduces "modular structures," encompassing important classes of algebraic and arithmetic interest, including Deligne structures, pure mixed *F*-isocrystals, and *F*-isocrystals with *F*-pure monodromy. The authors establish the boundedness of $L$-factors at special points for these structures, utilizing this result to derive the boundedness of $L$-factors associated with mixed *F*-sheaves, a core component relevant to the General Riemann Hypothesis. Furthermore, the findings confirm the boundedness of $L$-factors for modular fibrations, a category that integrates classical instances such as abelian and *K*-abelian fibrations.

This study explores spin transport in graphene nanostructures with armchair edges, focusing on their sensitivity to both Rashba and Dresselhaus spin-orbit coupling mechanisms. The analysis reveals that transport occurs via two channels: one driven by quantum Hall edge states and another arising from bulk states. While the edge state current is insensitive to spin orientation, the bulk current is fully spin-dependent. Consequently, an imbalance between upward and downward spin currents is generated, resulting in a non-zero Chern number. This phenomenon enables the creation of spin-sensitive, tunable conductance that can be regulated through gate voltage adjustments.

This article introduces two novel operators, $G$ and $T$, constructed from a continuous convex function $f: [0,1] \to [0,1]$. Specifically, $G$ is defined as $G(p) = (1-\lambda)p + \lambda f(p)$ and $T(p) = \min\{1, f(p)/\lambda\}$ for $p \in C[0,1]$, where $\lambda$ is a fixed constant in $(0,1)$. We establish that $G$ possesses monotonicity, continuity, linearity on the range of $f$, and that $T$ is also continuous and monotonic. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the operator $G$ exhibits a Korovkin-type property. In addition, the conditions under which the linear positive operator $G$ converges toward a target continuous function are analyzed.

In 1979, Erd\H{o}s, Gy\H{o}ri, and Simonovs introduced the concept of an independence quantity. Building on this foundation, we introduce a new graph invariant termed the Hamiltonian independence. Leveraging this new parameter, we establish a straightforward sufficient criterion for pancyclicity. Specifically, we demonstrate that if a simple undirected graph $G$ possesses $n$ vertices and its maximum independent set has a size strictly less than $\frac{n}{2}$, then $G$ is pancyclic.

This study examines the directed and guided flow of charged hadrons produced in Au+Au and isobar collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\text{NN}}}=200$ GeV. The analysis utilizes a novel technique to separate the contributions of flow driven by initial spatial eccentricity from that caused by magnetic fields. The results indicate that isobar collisions exhibit a smaller initial spatial eccentricity compared to both Au+Au and pp collisions, yet their magnetic fields are identical. Consequently, isobar pairs should display a flow difference reflecting the distinct balance between initial spatial eccentricity and the common magnetic field strength. The measured data aligns with this expectation, demonstrating that guided flow in Au+Au and isobar systems is consistent with predictions based on initial spatial eccentricity variations. Furthermore, the magnitude of the initial spatial ellipticity in isobar collisions is comparable to that in pp collisions, suggesting that the primary source of the observed directed flow in proton-proton collisions is guided flow rather than other mechanisms.

We introduce a novel Adaptive Sparse Grid-driven Spectral Koopman (ASGSK) method designed to enhance the computational efficiency of standard Spectral Koopman (SK) techniques. Recognizing that the primary bottleneck of SK approaches lies in the rapid expansion of high-dimensional Hamming cubes defining the lift space, we apply the Sparse Grid Skewb (SGSK) algorithm to construct an efficiently computed finite-dimensional invariant subspace. This algorithm leverages the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) to determine optimal expansion directions and incorporates the Subset Rule to maintain the necessary order of basis vectors for numerical integration. Furthermore, we utilize the Subset Rule to determine the specific columns of the dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) invariant operator, thereby enabling the targeted selection of dominant eigenvalues. Consequently, the resulting algorithm offers a highly effective strategy for approximating the Koopman operator, particularly within scenarios characterized by high dimensionality.

The traditional method for calculating the ionization of atoms and molecules in strong DC fields is the Outside-Inside-Outside (OIO) scheme. However, this approach encounters significant challenges when applied to molecules, particularly due to the need for multiple molecular orbitals and the computational complexity of solving the three-dimensional integral for the transition dipole moment. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a new Outside Complicated Scaling (OCS) method. This technique streamlines the overall computational process and significantly reduces the required memory. We have tested this method on hydrogen and hydrogen-like helium atoms, as well as hydrogen fluoride molecules, demonstrating that it yields results consistent with the OIO method.

The well-known Sinkhorn algorithm is a highly effective tool for rapidly computing optimal plans that solve the Schrödinger problem for systems governed by the Schrödinger equation. We demonstrate that this algorithm also converges in cases where such a solution does not exist, provided an appropriate variant of Wasserstein entropy is employed. Our findings are applicable to several other entropic metrics. Additionally, we establish a quasicontinuity property for these entropic distances.

The cross-section for the creation of $t\bar{t}$ pairs in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s} = 5.02$ TeV has been evaluated using data collected by the ATLAS detector at the LHC, accumulating an integrated luminosity of $25.3$ fb$^{-1}$. This analysis utilized a tag-and-probe strategy to identify dilepton events, specifically focusing on the $ee$ and $\mu\mu$ final states. Following background subtraction, the tag-and-probe technique was applied to determine the cross-section, yielding a result of $11.1 \pm 0.3$ (stat.) $\pm 0.4$ (syst.) pb. This measurement was subsequently benchmarked against theoretical predictions from Monte Carlo simulations, notably the POWHEG-PIERINI and ALPGEN-PIERINI models.

We investigate the localization behavior in a system of two interacting 1D disordered superconducting chains, where interactions occur exclusively at a single central site. Although this setup represents a minimal model for a Josephson junction box junction, the observed physics extends to any two-dimensional system featuring similar localized inter-chain coupling. Our findings indicate that when one chain is in a deeply localized regime, the system's energy spectrum is governed by an effective Hamiltonian describing the other chain as an Anderson model modified by a position-dependent, tunneling-induced phase. This phase shift originates from the localization state within the other chain and acts as a non-unitary perturbation. Consequently, this perturbation drives a transition between extended and localized regimes, creating a critical disorder threshold that depends on the eigenenergy of the already localized chain.

Human mobility and social interactions are vital to comprehending the dynamics of infectious disease outbreaks. This research utilizes mobile phone datasets to analyze shifts in urban activities during the pandemic, uncovering a significant correlation between income levels and behavioral patterns. Specifically, wealthier individuals exhibited reduced movement and fewer social engagements compared to their lower-income counterparts throughout the crisis. These disparities likely intensified economic imbalances, a finding that underscores the critical necessity of incorporating insights into urban dynamics to mitigate the socio-economic repercussions of this global health emergency.

This study introduces a novel field-separated preconditioner designed for linear systems arising from the conservative discretization of a two-phase flow equation. The approach utilizes a preconditioner composed of additive non-linear field-separated components, each tailored to a specific term in the original equation. A key advantage of Field-Separated Preconditioners (FSP) lies in their ability to decouple the solution process from the physical parameters, allowing for the efficient computation of multiple physical quantities using a single solution. While a field-separated variation of Anderson acceleration field-separated preconditioner (FSP) has been developed, it exhibits superior performance compared to field-separated preconditioner (FSP) alone. The study also examines the impact of varying grid resolutions and the nonlinear iteration count on solver efficiency.

This paper introduces a new class of optical devices designed to direct light from a bright source into a specific chiral configuration within a sample. Unlike traditional bilateral optical chambers, which illuminate both chiral forms equally, our unilateral chambers break this symmetry, producing distinct signals for left- and right-handed structures. The design leverages the unidirectional nature of topological edge states found in graphene metamaterials. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the chamber operates efficiently across the visible spectrum, and a practical implementation is proposed.

We examine the 2d Euclidean Liouville conformal field theory (LCFT) within the $JT$ gravity framework, specifically investigating its path integral on a genus-$g$ genus two surface ($g=2$) with a fixed metric. Adopting the perspective that the JT gravity path integral acts as a trace operation, we establish a correspondence between this trace and the matrix model partition function. By constructing a trace over an appropriate Fock space, we demonstrate the equivalence between this formulation and the matrix model's partition function. Building upon this equivalence, we evaluate the matrix partition function using coherent states, ultimately deriving its closed-form closed expression.

This study examines the influence of the cosmological constant on ideal fluid flat spacetime metrics designed for "warp travel"—regions of spacetime traversing by an observer within their own proper time. We demonstrate that within this framework, the cosmological constant can drive a fluid to reach its speed of light, causing its proper volume to contract to zero. We also derive new solutions featuring two distinct length scales, resulting in a characteristic transition time for the fluid's Lorentz contraction. Furthermore, we identify a fluid state capable of accelerating indefinitely, which occurs exclusively when the cosmological constant is negative.

Metropolitan data, such as geospatial information, are essential for urban research, yet the diverse formats, scales, and sources of this information often render it difficult to analyze. Resolving these challenges requires a unified data model, standardized citywide data schemas, and consistent data integration protocols. The GUIDE (Geospatial Urban Infrastructure Data Engineering Solutions) project seeks to address these hurdles by establishing a comprehensive framework for urban data engineering. The core of this framework is the City Data Model (CDM), a modular, hierarchical structure designed to accommodate various city data types. The primary objective of GUIDE is to lower the threshold for developing and deploying metropolitan data engineering applications.

We introduce a novel method for measuring the temperature of specific modes in an ion trap by observing the decay of the spin state of a single dopant. Experimental results from an experimental two-component (133Ba+ and 88Sr+) linear ion chain at NIST demonstrate that the dopant's spin relaxation rate is directly proportional to the kinetic energy of the nearest host's vibrational modes. We outline the underlying mechanisms of this relaxation and explore the implications for the design of quantum memory systems.

This study introduces a comprehensive quantum mechanical approach to evaluating tip-enhanced Raman spectroscopy, accounting for both the chemical and electromagnetic factors that drive signal amplification. This method facilitates a thorough analysis of the molecular and electronic properties of the sample and the interface between the sample and the tip. The thermodynamic behavior of $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{SO}_4$ has been investigated through a combination of differential scanning calorimetry, dielectric analysis, and first-principles calculations. Experimental results indicate that entropy variations associated with both the caloric cycle (involving $\text{NH}_4^{+}$ ion reorientation) and ferroelectric phase transition (driven by $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ ion flipping) are dominated by the configurational entropy of their respective ions. Furthermore, the computed entropy values derived from first-principles methods align closely with the experimentally measured data.

Reinforcement learning (RL) models have proven effective at replicating human learning patterns, yet the specific neural substrates responsible for these behaviors remain unclear. This study investigates whether distinct brain regions contribute to various RL strategies by examining their roles in execution. Using a fMRI task, researchers induced errors and corrections by dynamically adjusting reward probabilities, while tracking participants' choices and reaction times. A computational analysis revealed that suboptimal decision-making and rapid correction attempts activated overlapping brain circuits, specifically the striatum and midbrain. In contrast, attempts to optimize performance engaged a separate network centered on the prefrontal cortex and anterior cingulate. Crucially, midbrain activation correlated with both suboptimal choices and the magnitude of prediction errors, suggesting that the drive to avoid learning errors may inadvertently trigger suboptimal behaviors. These findings indicate that the pursuit of optimal outcomes recruits distinct circuits from those involved in suboptimal or characteristic responses.

The Approximate Close Neighbor Searching (ACNS) problem involves identifying the nearest neighbor for a query sequence $q$ within a dataset $S$ that is a collection of $n$ sequences, each of length $m$, where the proximity is defined by a cost metric. In this work, we examine the approximate Frechet distance, which measures similarity between two time-varying sequences. We present an approximate Frechet distance algorithm capable of locating a query's nearest neighbor within $S$ in $O(m^2n)$ time. This performance improves upon the current best known approach, which runs in $O(m^3n\epsilon^{-1})$ time. Furthermore, we establish a theoretical lower bound demonstrating that any ACNS algorithm for the approximate Frechet distance requires at least $\Omega(m^2n)$ time.

Scalable Error Mitigation (SEM) has recently emerged as a powerful strategy for enhancing the precision of quantum measurements. This work presents an iterative approach to SEM that effectively addresses current limitations in existing SEM protocols. We establish a theoretical framework that proves the validity of this method and demonstrate its efficacy through experiments with the iterative measurement of stabilizers within the surface code. Our findings indicate that this measurement error correction technique is viable for near-term fault-tolerant quantum computing applications.

This study introduces a methodology for designing control architectures that leverage inter-agent interactions to achieve collective goals. By utilizing a unified framework for both task and communication, the method ensures efficient coordination among autonomous entities. The underlying principle involves defining a reference model that encapsulates the desired collective behavior, which individual agents attempt to emulate through exchanged data. The proposed framework offers tools to define global objectives and local inter-agent mechanisms, enabling distributed control and consistent performance despite the absence of centralized oversight. This approach facilitates dynamic task assignment and the generation of coordinated patterns, such as formations. The method is demonstrated via simulation within a multi-robot setting where robots share position data to collectively reproduce a target pattern.

Conventional SLAM systems often fail in unfamiliar settings, such as during first-time robot exploration, because they depend on pre-existing maps. To address this, we introduce a new system capable of autonomous navigation in unknown environments by utilizing a hierarchical topological map. This map is constructed from a sequence of topological graphs, where each node represents a distinct substructure characterized by unique visual and geometric features. We evaluate the system's performance using both simulated and real-world scenarios featuring an omnidirectional vision sensor and a laser rangefinder. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves an average localization accuracy of 10.5 cm over distances exceeding 10 meters.

The construction of Z-array code sets is essential for developing DNA storage technologies. Previous second-generation DNA storage systems utilized the Z-array code set introduced in 2016, which relied on a single-variable function for its inter-group elements and a two-variable function for its internal elements. However, this approach resulted in an overly complex two-variable function that hindered practical application. To address this, we propose a new framework generating both code sets through two-variable functions, a method that ensures the inter-group elements are a subset of those within the 2-D Z-superimposable array code set. Our results demonstrate that this new architecture maintains the key properties required for DNA storage while offering greater feasibility for implementation.

X-ray tomography is a non-invasive imaging technique that reconstructs 3D material properties from 2D projections. While conventional X-ray CT relies on a single X-ray energy level, resulting in lower contrast and poorer resolution for low-atomic-number materials compared to methods using multiple energies, polyenergetic CT captures projections across several spectra to enhance image quality. However, this approach introduces significant noise and artifacts. This work introduces a novel optimization-based method for polyenergetic CT reconstruction that simultaneously handles data fitting, denoising, and the separation of materials based on their distinct atomic compositions. The proposed framework utilizes a unified objective function incorporating sparsity-promoting, total variation, and negative entropy regularizers. These regularizers are specifically tailored to improve signal-to-noise ratios and ensure non-negative reconstructions. Furthermore, the method includes an additional constraint that leverages the distinct X-ray attenuation characteristics of different materials to distinguish them effectively. The algorithm's efficacy is validated through numerical simulations and experimental data, with a specialized implementation designed for multi-material samples.

This work examines the optical characteristics of planar graphene plasmonics on a semiconductor substrate, specifically analyzing how local and electron-outflow-induced nonlocal effects influence the intervalley plasmon dispersion in the limit of vanishing gaps. We demonstrate that as the interval approaches zero, both nonlocal frameworks converge to identical results, predicting a 12% reduction in the plasmon mode's characteristic energy compared to predictions based on the Drude model. We also evaluate the influence of charge carrier density and the gap between graphene and the substrate on dispersion relations, finding that nonlocal corrections become significant only at extremely low carrier densities. Additionally, we assess the impact of a static electric field on dispersion, observing that nonlocal effects persist even when the graphene is decoupled from the substrate.

This study introduces a straightforward yet potent technique for addressing inchoic named entity recognition within the realm of context. The method functions by decomposing entity mentions into individual words, utilizing context to determine the significance of each word, and then aggregating these significance scores to estimate how crucial the complete entity mention is to the current context. The calculated importance metrics for entity mentions are subsequently integrated into the contextual NER framework. The approach relies on established techniques for entity mention decomposition as well as the calculation of significance and importance values for words and phrases. Empirical results indicate that incorporating this term-level importance feature into a BERT-based NER system yields substantial performance gains when dealing with mentions that lack contextual context.

Digital health records are gaining widespread adoption, yet the vast and varied nature of the accumulated data hinders effective analysis. Although deep learning has shown promise in processing such information, it often fails to account for data heterogeneity, which is a critical factor in the digital health context. To address this, we introduce the Diverse Similarity Graph Neural Network (DSGNN), a data-driven framework designed to capture the domain-specific similarities inherent in digital health records. By integrating a similarity matrix with a graph neural network, DSGNN effectively addresses both the heterogeneity of the data and its sequential characteristics. We evaluated this model using a digital health record dataset to classify patients with type 2 diabetes, demonstrating that it outperforms existing methods. Furthermore, case studies highlight the model's ability to uncover novel insights, such as identifying specific patient subgroups with distinct disease trajectories.

This study investigates how interfacial polarization affects the structure of the electric double layer (EDL) adjacent to a charged, soft interface within an electrolyte solution. Using Density Functional Theory (DFT), we modeled a dextran dextran-like polymer layer grafted with charged side chains. Our findings reveal that polarization significantly alters the EDL architecture: a solvent dipole oriented oppositely to an external electric field creates a localized dipolar layer near the interface, which weakens as field strength increases. This orientation generates a potential minimum for dipolar molecules, promoting their confinement to the boundary and enhancing the development of charge overscreening and oscillations characteristic of the EDL. Conversely, molar concentration variations of the solvent cause only minor shifts in the potential minimum's location, indicating that concentration plays a limited role compared to the field effect. These insights offer critical understanding for designing soft materials and interfaces with tailored properties for applications in biotechnology and energy storage.

We introduce a novel methodology for automatically generating software specifications by processing textual materials such as requirements, news articles, and technical blogs. This method leverages existing semantic web technologies to automatically extract imperative elements (commands) and state components (conditions) from unstructured text. The approach involves learning the textual patterns associated with these concepts using a dataset of manually annotated textual samples. By utilizing semantic web standards, we can automatically tag source materials at the syntactic and semantic levels to identify imperative sections. Subsequently, these specifications are derived directly from the textual specifications and distributed across various software repositories.

This study introduces an energy-efficient collaboration network coding framework, combining network coding with a joint approach to relay timetabling and power allocation. In collaboration network coding, geographically proximate wireless nodes jointly encode their transmitted data. To minimize energy consumption, we first address relay timetabling by determining the optimal relay assignment for each link within a specific time slot. Subsequently, network coding is applied to paired relays during that interval. For power distribution, we simultaneously optimize transmit power levels at both source and relay to reduce total energy usage. The resulting optimization challenge is formulated as a mixed-integer non-convex program. To resolve this, we develop a suboptimal solution using subgradient descent methods, which iteratively alternate between timetabling decisions and power control updates. Numerical results demonstrate that the energy savings achieved by our proposed framework surpass those of conventional network coding approaches that do not utilize relay collaboration.

This study examines the magnetic and electronic characteristics of Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states arising from a Mn impurity on a Nb(110) superconductor. We employ relativistic first-principles calculations to map the $k$-dependent local density of states, accounting for the strong hybridization between the localized $3d$ orbitals of the Mn atom and Nb conduction electrons. The analysis reveals that the YSR states exhibit orbital selectivity, with the $z$-oriented $3d$ orbital exhibiting the strongest coupling to the superconducting continuum. Furthermore, the orbital selectivity of these states is sensitive to interorbital exchange interactions, which are determined by the specific electronic and structural environment of the adsorbate.

This study reports the outcomes of an initial investigation into the rare decay process $K^+\rightarrow\pi^+\nu\bar{\nu}$, which was conducted using the Decay-In-Motion technique at the CERN H1 beam. Data were collected over a period of 100 days, accumulating a total of $1.09 \times 10^{11}$ identified kaons. The analysis targets the specific kinematic region where the kaon decays into a single neutrino-antineutrino pair, corresponding to an invisible final state. No such events were observed; consequently, an upper limit on the branching fraction of $6.6 \times 10^{-12}$ was established at a 90% confidence level.

Pre-train, deep neural network filters are commonly employed to reduce bias in distribution-to-distribution distribution alignment. However, these filters often result in the loss of discriminative information, which can hinder downstream tasks. This study introduces a new approach to aligning distributions that integrates a deep convolutional network with a feature selection component. The model is designed to filter out prejudicial data while retaining discriminative features. The model's performance was evaluated on a face recognition dataset, where it demonstrated significant mitigation of racial bias.

Satellite imagery is increasingly utilized for monitoring changes in the landscape, such as urban development and deforestation. While deep learning methods have become the standard for image analysis, they often suffer from excessive model sizes and high computational demands. This paper introduces a novel image processing technique capable of identifying edges in satellite pictures without relying on deep neural networks. The method's performance was evaluated against the popular COHO dataset using two distinct configurations. The results indicate that this non-deep approach achieves edge detection accuracy nearly on par with state-of-the-art deep models.

Non-linear X-ray absorption near-edge absorption (NL-XANES) offers a promising avenue for investigating electron-gating mechanisms and high-field electron dynamics within matter. This study introduces a rate model to characterize NL-XANES, utilizing it to examine electron gating dynamics in diatomic molecules. By examining the NL-XANES signatures of $N_2$ and $CO$ under intense X-ray illumination, the research demonstrates that NL-XANES can sensitively probe spatial electron gating dynamics. Furthermore, the proposed framework is applicable to NL-XANES investigations across a broad spectrum of materials.

Resiliency is a critical requirement for real-time communication systems, particularly in mobile environments where hostile activities such as modulation categorization (ModCat) can disrupt operations. In this context, Deep Learning (DL) has emerged as a promising solution for performing ModCat; however, recent studies have demonstrated its vulnerability to adversarial attacks. This research introduces the first-ever exploration of adversarial attacks targeting DL-based ModCat, specifically focusing on white-box scenarios. We evaluate three attack methodologies: poison, evasion, and transfer attacks. Our findings indicate that poison attacks can degrade the performance of state-of-the-art ModCat with a success rate exceeding 90%. Furthermore, we observe that transfer attacks achieve a 70% success rate in white-box settings, while white-box transfer attacks reach an 80% success rate. To address these vulnerabilities and enhance robustness, we propose the Blend GAN, a novel deep generative model designed to strengthen ModCat against such attacks. Experimental results confirm that our method improves resilience to poison attacks by 10.5% and to transfer attacks by 13.5%.

Segmentation of brain lesions in multiple sclerosis (MS) aids in diagnosing the condition and tracking disease progression. While deep learning has largely replaced traditional image processing methods for this task, adapting pre-trained models to a clinic's specific data often requires continuing education. This study evaluates continuous learning against training from scratch by using a U-Net architecture pre-trained on 1,025 multiple sclerosis lesions. Experiments were conducted across three datasets containing 150, 200, and 400 lesions respectively. Continuous learning was implemented via a standard Adam optimizer with an learning rate of 0.001, while the training-from-scratch baseline utilized Adam with an learning rate of 0.001. The findings indicate that continuous learning consistently outperforms training from scratch, achieving Dice coefficients of 0.752 and 0.742 versus 0.702 and 0.702 on the two largest datasets. Additionally, continuous learning offers superior computational efficiency, reducing training time by 96% and requiring 96% less GPU memory.

This study introduces Manic contrast, a new method for image enhancement designed to improve low-quality images with poor visual quality. The approach utilizes a dual-branch architecture: a detail branch responsible for recovering fine structures and a texture branch focused on refining surface characteristics. To ensure high-quality outputs, we formulated an enhancement loss combining perceptual metrics with an adversarial loss component. Additionally, we established a self-distillation framework to facilitate unsupervised training. Extensive testing on various image enhancement tasks demonstrates that the method achieves superior results compared to existing techniques.

This study introduces a mathematical framework for dynamical systems that addresses machine intelligence regarding modeling errors. We establish a non-linear autonomous dynamical system to evolve the state of an "agent" autonomous machine, where the driving force is the fixed dynamics of a target system and the state represents the agent's predictive accuracy. This system models an agent learning to anticipate its environment, where the system dynamics and their associated uncertainties are fixed within the mathematical description. We provide a proof that these errors converge to stable equilibria, demonstrating that the agent can effectively learn and minimize modeling errors. This work constitutes a foundational step toward analyzing dynamical systems equipped with autonomous machines capable of self-governing error adaptation.

This study investigates the core structure of the infrared dark nebula (IND) Dragon, utilizing 24 $\mu$m observations from the Spitzer Space Telescope and 850 $\mu$m data from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA). The spatial resolution of the ALMA data (0.03 pc) is sufficient to resolve the IND Dragon's core, which exhibits a central density of $10^7$ cm$^{-3}$ and a mass of $10^5$ M$_{\odot}$. The core displays a dense central region surrounded by a more diffuse outer envelope. Additionally, the source is characterized by a high aspect ratio, with a major axis of 1.2 pc and a minor axis of 0.1 pc. The observed 850 $\mu$m emission spectrum shows a central peak that is significantly narrower than the outer source structure, indicating that the IND Dragon's core is optically thick. This optical depth suggests that the source is more massive than previously estimated, with a total mass of $10^6$ M$_{\odot}$. The source exhibits a high mass-to-flux ratio of 100, which is indicative of magnetic flux accumulation. The accumulation of magnetic flux and the associated collapse of the IND Dragon core are likely to facilitate the formation of massive stars.

Primordial black holes (PBHs) represent a compelling candidate for dark matter, distinguished by their lack of electromagnetic interactions and the potential for significant gravitational wave signals. This study investigates dark matter annihilation profiles around PBHs, a process that could enhance the prospects for detecting positrons and gamma rays in upcoming experiments. We executed PBH distribution simulations within galactic dark matter using PopSyCLE, a modular framework designed for population and system simulations in exoplanets and dark matter environments. The analysis reveals that the internal structure of the dark matter halo significantly influences the PBH distribution and, consequently, the annihilation profile. Specifically, an adiabatic cusp profile results in a substantially higher PBH concentration near the galactic center compared to an isothermal profile. Furthermore, we examined the impact of PBH density variations on annihilation signals, noting that an increased PBH density amplifies the observed flux. These findings underscore the critical necessity of incorporating PBHs into dark matter distribution models to accurately predict observable signatures.

This study examines the mechanical behavior of a chain formed by identical, rigid wedges, where each individual wedge is modeled as a collection of touching spheres. The system's configuration is defined by the positions of the wedges' axes, which are constrained to lie within a two-dimensional plane. Unlike the initial wedges fixed by boundary conditions, the axes of the internal intermediates are determined by minimizing the system's total potential energy. Our analysis reveals that the system's potential energy consists of two components: a repulsive term resulting from the interaction between spheres and an effective potential representing the entropic cost of the degrees of freedom associated with the intermediate wedges' orientations. The magnitude of this enthalpic contribution depends on the number of spheres constituting each wedge. The system exhibits two distinct stable states: a linear stage and a splay stage. In the linear stage, all wedges align along a straight line, whereas the splay stage is characterized by the presence of local orientational order. Furthermore, the transition between these stages is governed by the wedges' internal composition; specifically, adding more spheres to each wedge stabilizes the linear configuration.

Parameter-efficient tuning recently emerged as a method to fine-tune large pre-trained models (PMs) by adjusting only a minimal subset of parameters, offering advantages in speed and resource usage compared to full fine-tuning. However, this approach often underperforms relative to complete fine-tuning. We hypothesize that this gap arises because unique tokens in training data act as effective indicators of specific task characteristics, allowing the model to adapt uniquely per task while retaining most pre-trained knowledge. To validate this, we introduce Unique Token Adaptation (UTA), a method that assigns a distinct token to each task and adjusts just these tokens along with a small number of parameters within the adapter layers. We further present a novel, efficient, and scalable strategy to generate these unique tokens automatically. Evaluated on six benchmarks, UTA achieves results on par with full fine-tuning and significantly surpasses other parameter-efficient techniques.

This study introduces two contrast relations to address preference ordering among subsets drawn from distinct collections, each containing augmenting sets from potentially different underlying collections. While these contrasts align in core principles, they differ in specific operational details. We demonstrate that the contrast ordering associated with the first contrast relation constitutes a partial order, whereas the one derived from the second relation exhibits only a partial preorder structure. We establish two theorems to demonstrate the conditions under which this preorder evolves into a full partial order. Additionally, we explore connections between preference subset augmentation and contrast relations, proving that any such subset augmentation problem corresponds to at least one contrast relation, with preferences determined by the sizes of these subsets. We further present two conjectures suggesting sufficient conditions under which an existing contrast can be transformed into another where the resulting preference order is identical.

This study investigates the dynamic and thermodynamic characteristics of a polymer system across the entire temperature range, encompassing both equilibrium and deeply supercooled liquid states. We demonstrate that two distinct thermodynamic potentials are essential to characterize dynamics in these materials: one to describe equilibrium behavior and another to address the glass transition. Furthermore, we establish a critical connection between these potentials and specific dynamics inherent to glass transition phenomena. Our findings confirm that the spatial and temporal evolution of local equilibrium during this transition is governed by the gradient of free energy density and temporal changes in specific heat capacity.

Transformer-based language models have achieved remarkable success, yet their training remains highly expensive. This paper introduces a training strategy that leverages the inductive biases of Transformers to reduce costs by approximately 50% without compromising model performance. Our method involves a two-stage process: initially, the Transformer is trained on a dataset of a fixed size, followed by a rejection phase where the model is retrained on an expanded corpus, deliberately excluding any data seen in the first stage. We find that this retraining on non-overlapping vocabulary significantly enhances convergence speed, leading to final results that match or exceed those of continuous training on the full dataset. Empirical evaluations demonstrate the method's efficacy across various model scales and linguistic resources.

Neural machine interpretation generates human-readable explanations for software defects using natural language. Although these models produce explanations that are accurate and diverse, they often overlook critical code context, leading to irrelevant or imprecise details. To address this, we introduce a look-ahead attention mechanism that guides the model to select more pertinent source code information. Evaluating our approach on the Kullback-Leibler Diverse and Levenshtein Edit Distance metrics demonstrates significant improvements in contextual relevance and overall performance.

We demonstrate an innovative method for deriving the Kontsevich weights of relation graphs through curvature graphs, a calculation validated for specific illustrative instances.
